cards.q: What defines a graded potential?
cards.a: A membrane potential change whose size varies with stimulus strength.
options: A membrane potential change whose size varies with stimulus strength
A membrane potential change of fixed size once threshold is crossed
A membrane potential change carried by voltage gated Na+ channels
A membrane potential change that spreads without losing any size
cards.explanation: A graded potential is produced when gated channels open and let ions cross, and the more channels that open, the larger the voltage change, so its size reports stimulus strength. A change of fixed size once threshold is crossed describes the action potential, which is all or none. Voltage gated Na+ channels drive the action potential upstroke, while graded potentials come mostly from chemically and mechanically gated channels. Spreading without losing size describes regenerative propagation down an axon, not the decremental spread of a graded potential.

cards.q: In a typical multipolar neuron, where are graded potentials mainly produced?
cards.a: On the dendrites and cell body.
options: At the nodes of Ranvier along the axon
On the dendrites and cell body
At the trigger zone where voltage gated Na+ channels cluster
Along the myelinated internodes of the axon
cards.explanation: Dendrites and the cell body carry the chemically gated channels that synaptic transmitters open, so this is where postsynaptic graded potentials arise and then spread toward the trigger zone. The nodes of Ranvier and the trigger zone are dense in voltage gated Na+ channels and are where action potentials are generated and regenerated. Myelinated internodes are insulated and have very few channels of any kind, which is exactly why current passes them without much leak.

cards.q: At a chemical synapse, which class of ion channel opens to produce the postsynaptic graded potential?
cards.a: Chemically gated channels.
options: Chemically gated channels
Voltage gated Na+ channels
Mechanically gated channels
Voltage gated K+ channels
cards.explanation: A neurotransmitter binds a receptor and opens chemically gated (ligand gated) channels, and the ion flow through them is what shifts the postsynaptic membrane potential. Mechanically gated channels do produce graded potentials, but in sensory receptors responding to stretch or pressure, not at a chemical synapse. Voltage gated Na+ and K+ channels respond to membrane potential rather than transmitter, and they shape the action potential once the graded potential reaches the trigger zone.

cards.q: What is an excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP)?
cards.a: A graded depolarization that moves the membrane toward threshold.
options: A graded hyperpolarization that moves the membrane away from threshold
An all or none depolarization generated at the trigger zone
A graded depolarization that moves the membrane toward threshold
A steady depolarization that lasts as long as the stimulus without decay
cards.explanation: An EPSP is a local depolarization, usually from Na+ entry through chemically gated channels, that brings the membrane potential closer to threshold and so raises the chance of firing. A graded hyperpolarization is the inhibitory postsynaptic potential, the IPSP, which does the opposite. An all or none depolarization at the trigger zone is the action potential itself. EPSPs are brief and decay both over time and over distance, so a steady undecaying response does not describe them.

cards.q: Which ion movement most often produces an inhibitory postsynaptic potential?
cards.a: Cl- moving into the cell.
options: Cl- moving into the cell
Ca2+ moving into the cell
K+ moving into the cell
Na+ moving into the cell
cards.explanation: Cl- entry adds negative charge to the inside of the cell, hyperpolarizing it and pushing the membrane potential away from threshold. K+ movement also hyperpolarizes, but K+ leaves the cell rather than entering, since its gradient points outward. Na+ entry and Ca2+ entry both add positive charge inside and are depolarizing, so they produce excitatory rather than inhibitory potentials.

cards.q: In the spread of a graded potential, what does current leak refer to?
cards.a: Positive charge escaping back across the membrane through open channels.
options: Positive charge escaping back across the membrane through open channels
Ions being pumped back out by the Na+/K+ ATPase
Charge lost to the friction of the cytosol as current flows lengthwise
Current passing to a neighboring cell through gap junctions
cards.explanation: As charge spreads sideways inside the cell, some of it slips back out across the membrane through open leak channels, so less and less current is left to change the potential farther along. Charge lost to the friction of the cytosol is the other factor, cytoplasmic resistance, and the two act together. The Na+/K+ ATPase restores concentration gradients over minutes and is far too slow to shape a single graded potential. Gap junction current is a feature of electrical synapses, not of decay within one neuron.

cards.q: What does the term cytoplasmic resistance describe?
cards.a: The opposition the cytosol offers to current flowing lengthwise inside the cell.
options: The opposition the cytosol offers to current flowing lengthwise inside the cell
The opposition the membrane offers to ions crossing from inside to outside
The opposition the extracellular fluid offers to current returning to the source
The opposition myelin offers to charge leaking out of the internode
cards.explanation: Cytoplasm is a conductor, but a poor one, so current spreading lengthwise inside a dendrite or axon loses strength the farther it has to travel. The opposition of the membrane to ions crossing it is membrane resistance, which is the property that leak channels lower and myelin raises. Extracellular fluid does carry the return current, but its resistance is small and is not what the term names. Myelin insulation raises membrane resistance rather than cytoplasmic resistance.

cards.q: As a graded potential spreads away from the point where it started, what happens to its amplitude?
cards.a: It gets smaller with distance.
options: It grows larger with distance
It stays the same at every distance
It reverses sign a short distance away
It gets smaller with distance
cards.explanation: Graded potentials spread passively, and current leaks out across the membrane while the cytoplasm resists flow, so the voltage change shrinks the farther it travels. This decay is why a graded potential can only signal over short distances and why neurons need action potentials for long ones. An amplitude that stays constant describes a regenerating action potential, which is rebuilt at every point along the axon. Nothing in passive spread flips the sign of the potential, and growth with distance would require an energy source that passive spread does not have.

cards.q: A stimulus opens twice as many chemically gated channels as before on a dendrite. What is the result?
cards.a: A graded potential of larger amplitude.
options: A graded potential of the same amplitude that spreads faster
A graded potential of larger amplitude
A graded potential of the same amplitude repeated twice
An action potential of larger amplitude at the trigger zone
cards.explanation: More open channels means more ions crossing per unit time, more charge moved, and therefore a bigger voltage change, which is exactly what makes graded potentials graded. Passive spread speed is set by the cable properties of the cell, not by how many channels the stimulus opened. Nothing about a stronger stimulus splits the response into two events. The action potential option is the classic trap: a bigger graded potential can make an action potential more likely, but it never makes the action potential itself bigger, because that response is all or none.

cards.q: Two EPSPs arrive at the same synapse two milliseconds apart, and the second builds on the tail of the first. What is this called?
cards.a: Temporal summation.
options: Spatial summation
Temporal summation
Divergence to two targets
Convergence of two pathways
cards.explanation: Two inputs at one location arriving close together in time overlap before the first decays, and their depolarizations add, which is temporal summation. Spatial summation is the same addition, but of inputs arriving at the same moment from different locations on the neuron. Convergence and divergence describe wiring patterns, how many neurons feed into one cell or how many cells one neuron contacts, not the adding of overlapping potentials.

cards.q: Two different presynaptic neurons fire at the same instant onto separate dendrites, and their EPSPs add at the trigger zone. What is this called?
cards.a: Spatial summation.
options: Temporal summation
Facilitation of a single synapse
Spatial summation
Recruitment of additional axons
cards.explanation: Inputs at different places on the same neuron arriving at the same moment sum where their spreading currents meet, and that is spatial summation. Temporal summation would require the inputs to be separated in time at one site rather than separated in space at one instant. Facilitation describes a synapse becoming more effective with use, which is a change in one synapse rather than the addition of two. Recruitment refers to bringing more axons into a population response, which happens across cells, not within one postsynaptic neuron.

cards.q: An EPSP measured at the dendrite is 15 mV, but at the trigger zone 500 micrometers away it is only 4 mV. What best explains the drop?
cards.a: Charge leaked out across the membrane while the cytoplasm resisted the flow.
options: The Na+/K+ ATPase pumped the excess Na+ back out along the way
Voltage gated Na+ channels inactivated partway down the dendrite
Charge leaked out across the membrane while the cytoplasm resisted the flow
The membrane entered a refractory period between the two recording sites
cards.explanation: Passive spread loses current two ways at once: some charge escapes through open membrane channels, and the cytosol resists the lengthwise flow of what is left, so the recorded voltage falls steadily with distance. The Na+/K+ ATPase works on a timescale of many seconds to minutes and cannot account for a change occurring in a fraction of a millisecond. Voltage gated Na+ channels are sparse on dendrites and are not what carries a spreading EPSP. Refractory periods follow action potentials, and no action potential has occurred here.

cards.q: One dendrite is twice the diameter of another, which lowers its cytoplasmic resistance. How far does a graded potential spread in the wider one?
cards.a: Farther, because less current is lost to internal resistance.
options: A shorter distance, because the larger volume dilutes the charge
Farther, but only if the dendrite is myelinated
The same distance, because diameter affects only action potentials
Farther, because less current is lost to internal resistance
cards.explanation: A wider cylinder of cytoplasm is an easier path for current, the same way a wide pipe carries water with less pressure loss, so more of the original charge reaches a given distance and the potential decays less. Charge is not diluted by volume in any way that matters here; what matters is the resistance of the path. Diameter affects passive spread in every process, which is why it also affects action potential conduction velocity. Myelin helps by reducing leak across the membrane, but the diameter effect is real with or without it.

cards.q: A toxin holds extra K+ leak channels open along a dendrite. What happens to the distance a graded potential can spread?
cards.a: It becomes shorter, because more current escapes across the membrane.
options: It becomes longer, because K+ carries the signal along the dendrite
It becomes shorter, because more current escapes across the membrane
It stays the same, because leak channels do not carry current
It becomes longer, because the resting potential is now more stable
cards.explanation: Extra open channels lower membrane resistance, so spreading current has more escape routes and the potential dies out over a shorter distance. K+ leaving through leak channels carries charge out of the cell rather than along it; the lengthwise carrier of a graded potential is current flowing through the cytoplasm. Leak channels certainly do carry current, and that is exactly the problem. A more stable resting potential is not an advantage for spread, since the cost of stability here is a shorter distance.

cards.q: An EPSP of 6 mV and an IPSP of 4 mV reach the trigger zone at the same moment. What is the net change in membrane potential?
cards.a: About 2 mV of depolarization.
options: About 10 mV of depolarization
No net change, since opposite inputs cancel completely
About 2 mV of hyperpolarization
About 2 mV of depolarization
cards.explanation: Graded potentials sum algebraically, so a 6 mV depolarization plus a 4 mV hyperpolarization leaves roughly 2 mV of net depolarization. Adding the two magnitudes to get 10 mV would treat the inhibitory input as if it were excitatory. A net hyperpolarization would require the IPSP to be the larger of the two, which it is not. Complete cancellation happens only when the two are equal in size, so it is the right answer for a 4 mV EPSP paired with a 4 mV IPSP, not for this pair.

cards.q: A graded potential is 20 mV at the synapse, 11 mV at 250 micrometers, and 5 mV at the trigger zone 500 micrometers away, where 15 mV of depolarization is needed to reach threshold. Does an action potential fire?
cards.a: No, because the signal decays to 5 mV, below the 15 mV needed.
options: Yes, because the graded potential is regenerated at the trigger zone
No, because the signal decays to 5 mV, below the 15 mV needed
No, because graded potentials cannot depolarize a trigger zone at all
Yes, because 20 mV of depolarization was reached at the synapse
cards.explanation: What matters is the voltage that actually arrives at the trigger zone, and after leak and cytoplasmic resistance have taken their toll only 5 mV is left, which is well short of the 15 mV required. Graded potentials are not regenerated as they spread; that is the defining difference from an action potential. They do depolarize the trigger zone, just not always enough, so the claim that they cannot is too strong. The 20 mV at the synapse is real but irrelevant, because threshold is judged where the voltage gated Na+ channels actually sit.

cards.q: A drug lowers the number of open leak channels in a neuron's dendrites without changing its synaptic channels. Predict the effect on the neuron's response to a weak synaptic input.
cards.a: It becomes more likely to fire, because graded potentials spread farther.
options: It becomes less likely to fire, because the dendrite now holds less charge
It is unchanged, because leak channels act only at the resting potential
It becomes more likely to fire, because graded potentials spread farther
It becomes less likely to fire, because threshold at the trigger zone rises
cards.explanation: Fewer open leak channels means higher membrane resistance, so less current escapes on the way and a larger fraction of the original depolarization survives the trip to the trigger zone, making threshold easier to reach. Reduced leak does not reduce the charge delivered by the synapse; it preserves it. Leak channels operate at every membrane potential, not just at rest, and they are precisely what drains a spreading graded potential. Threshold is set by the voltage gated Na+ channels at the trigger zone and does not shift because dendritic leak changed.

cards.q: Two synapses each deliver an EPSP that is 9 mV by the time it reaches the trigger zone, where 15 mV of depolarization is needed. What determines whether an action potential occurs?
cards.a: Whether the two EPSPs arrive close enough in time to overlap and sum.
options: Whether each EPSP alone is larger than the resting potential
Whether the axon is myelinated along its first segment
Whether the Na+/K+ ATPase has restored the gradients between inputs
Whether the two EPSPs arrive close enough in time to overlap and sum
cards.explanation: Nine millivolts alone falls short, so firing depends on summation: if the second EPSP arrives while the first is still decaying, the two add to roughly 18 mV and threshold is crossed, and if it arrives too late the membrane has already returned toward rest. Comparing an EPSP to the resting potential is not a meaningful test, since what matters is the distance from rest to threshold. Myelination changes conduction speed past the trigger zone but does not decide whether threshold is reached there. The pump restores gradients far too slowly to matter over the few milliseconds in question.

cards.q: A neuron's synapses release normal amounts of transmitter and the EPSP recorded right at the synapse is normal, yet the EPSP arriving at the trigger zone is unusually small. Which change best explains this?
cards.a: A longer and narrower dendrite between the synapse and the trigger zone.
options: A higher density of voltage gated Na+ channels at the trigger zone
A greater number of transmitter receptors on the postsynaptic membrane
A longer and narrower dendrite between the synapse and the trigger zone
A lower resting permeability to K+ across the dendritic membrane
cards.explanation: The loss happens between the two recording points, so the explanation has to be in the cable properties of the path: extra length gives leak more opportunity, and a narrower dendrite raises cytoplasmic resistance, and together they shrink what arrives. More receptors would enlarge the EPSP at the synapse, which the question says is normal. More Na+ channels at the trigger zone would lower the depolarization needed to fire but would not change the size of the potential arriving. Lower K+ permeability means less leak, which would deliver a larger signal, the opposite of what is observed.

cards.q: Which ion movement produces the rapid depolarization from threshold to the peak of an action potential?
cards.a: Na+ moving into the cell.
options: K+ moving out of the cell
Cl- moving into the cell
Na+ moving into the cell
Ca2+ moving out of the cell
cards.explanation: At threshold, voltage gated Na+ channels open and Na+ rushes in down both its concentration and its electrical gradient, carrying positive charge inward and driving the membrane potential sharply upward. K+ moving out is the repolarizing current that follows, not the upstroke. Cl- entry would hyperpolarize the cell. Ca2+ exit is a slow pump and exchanger process that has no role in the neuronal upstroke.

cards.q: Which ion movement produces repolarization after the peak of an action potential?
cards.a: K+ moving out of the cell.
options: K+ moving out of the cell
Cl- moving out of the cell
Na+ moving out of the cell
K+ moving into the cell
cards.explanation: Voltage gated K+ channels open late, and with the inside of the cell now positive, K+ leaves rapidly down both gradients, carrying positive charge out and driving the potential back toward rest. Na+ does not exit through channels during repolarization; the Na+ channels inactivate, which stops the inward current but does not reverse it. Cl- exit would add positive charge inside, which is depolarizing. K+ entering the cell would work against its steep outward gradient.

cards.q: What produces the afterhyperpolarization at the end of an action potential?
cards.a: Voltage gated K+ channels stay open past the return to the resting potential.
options: Voltage gated K+ channels stay open past the return to the resting potential
The Na+/K+ ATPase pumps out extra Na+ during this interval
Cl- channels open and drive the potential below rest
Voltage gated Na+ channels reopen briefly and carry current in reverse
cards.explanation: Voltage gated K+ channels are slow to close, so K+ keeps leaving after the potential has already reached rest, pulling the membrane closer to the K+ equilibrium potential near -90 mV before the channels finally shut. The Na+/K+ ATPase does move net positive charge out, but it contributes only a few millivolts continuously and does not create this transient dip. Cl- channels are not gated by voltage in this way in a typical axon. Na+ channels do not run in reverse; after inactivation they simply stop conducting until the membrane repolarizes.

cards.q: How many gates does a voltage gated Na+ channel have, and what are they called?
cards.a: Two, an activation gate and an inactivation gate.
options: One, an activation gate
Two, a chemical gate and a voltage gate
Two, an activation gate and an inactivation gate
Three, one for each phase of the action potential
cards.explanation: The voltage gated Na+ channel has a fast activation gate that opens on depolarization and a slower inactivation gate that swings shut a fraction of a millisecond later, and this two gate design is what makes the upstroke brief and self limiting. A single gate would let Na+ keep flowing until the membrane repolarized, and there would be no absolute refractory period. Chemically gated channels have a binding site rather than a second gate. Nothing about the channel provides one gate per phase; the K+ channel, with its single slow gate, handles repolarization.

cards.q: At the peak of the action potential, what is the state of most voltage gated Na+ channels?
cards.a: Inactivated, with the inactivation gate closed.
options: Open, with both gates open
Inactivated, with the inactivation gate closed
Resting, with the activation gate closed and the inactivation gate open
Open, but no longer conducting because the driving force is zero
cards.explanation: The inactivation gate closes about a millisecond after depolarization begins, which shuts off Na+ entry and is a major reason the potential turns around at the peak rather than climbing to the Na+ equilibrium potential. Fully open channels describe the rising phase, before inactivation catches up. The resting configuration, activation gate closed and inactivation gate open, is the state at -70 mV and the state the channel must return to before it can fire again. Driving force on Na+ is smaller at the peak but is not zero, since the peak falls short of the Na+ equilibrium potential.

cards.q: What is the approximate peak membrane potential of a neuronal action potential?
cards.a: About +30 mV.
options: About -55 mV
About 0 mV
About +30 mV
About +60 mV
cards.explanation: The peak lands near +30 mV, positive inside but short of the Na+ equilibrium potential because K+ channels are opening and Na+ channels are inactivating before the membrane can get there. About -55 mV is threshold, the potential at which the upstroke starts rather than where it ends. Zero millivolts is passed on the way up but is not the peak. About +60 mV is the Na+ equilibrium potential, the value the peak approaches but never reaches.

cards.q: What is the typical resting membrane potential of a neuron?
cards.a: About -70 mV.
options: About -90 mV
About -30 mV
About -55 mV
About -70 mV
cards.explanation: A neuron rests near -70 mV, set mainly by the high resting permeability to K+ with a small steady Na+ leak pulling it slightly positive of the K+ equilibrium potential. About -90 mV is that K+ equilibrium potential, the value the membrane approaches during afterhyperpolarization. About -55 mV is threshold, not rest. About -30 mV is well past threshold, and a neuron sitting there would already have fired or be inactivated.

cards.q: Which channel is slow to open and slow to close during an action potential?
cards.a: The voltage gated K+ channel.
options: The voltage gated Na+ channel
The voltage gated K+ channel
The K+ leak channel
The chemically gated Na+ channel
cards.explanation: The voltage gated K+ channel responds sluggishly to depolarization, which is why repolarization lags the upstroke, and it is slow to shut, which is why the membrane overshoots into afterhyperpolarization. The voltage gated Na+ channel is the fast one, opening within a fraction of a millisecond and inactivating almost as quickly. Leak channels are not gated at all; they are open at rest and do not change with voltage. Chemically gated channels open when transmitter binds and have no role in shaping the action potential waveform.

cards.q: At a resting potential of -70 mV, what is the position of the two gates on a voltage gated Na+ channel?
cards.a: Activation gate closed, inactivation gate open.
options: Activation gate open, inactivation gate open
Activation gate open, inactivation gate closed
Activation gate closed, inactivation gate closed
Activation gate closed, inactivation gate open
cards.explanation: At rest the channel is closed but ready: the activation gate blocks the pore, while the inactivation gate is standing open so the channel can conduct the instant depolarization swings the activation gate aside. Both gates open is the brief conducting state during the upstroke. Activation open with inactivation closed is the inactivated state that follows the peak and blocks further firing. Both gates closed is not a state the channel occupies, because the inactivation gate closes only after depolarization has opened the activation gate.

cards.q: A drug blocks most voltage gated K+ channels in an axon. What happens to the action potential?
cards.a: Repolarization is slowed and the action potential is prolonged.
options: The upstroke is abolished and no action potential occurs
The resting potential becomes more negative than usual
The peak is lower but the timing is unchanged
Repolarization is slowed and the action potential is prolonged
cards.explanation: Repolarization depends on K+ leaving through those channels, so blocking them removes the main outward current and the membrane crawls back toward rest, stretching the action potential and blunting or erasing the afterhyperpolarization. Abolishing the upstroke would require blocking Na+ channels instead. The peak is set by Na+ entry and by how quickly it is opposed, so it is unchanged or slightly higher, not lower. Losing K+ permeability moves the resting potential in the depolarized direction if anything, not the hyperpolarized one.

cards.q: Why does the membrane potential swing positive during the upstroke of an action potential?
cards.a: Na+ permeability briefly exceeds K+ permeability, so Vm heads toward the Na+ equilibrium.
options: Na+ permeability briefly exceeds K+ permeability, so Vm heads toward the Na+ equilibrium
The Na+/K+ ATPase temporarily reverses and pumps Na+ into the cell instead of out
The Na+ concentration inside the cell rises above the concentration outside it
K+ channels close completely, leaving almost no charge able to cross the membrane at all
cards.explanation: Membrane potential always drifts toward the equilibrium potential of whichever ion is currently most permeant, and during the upstroke open Na+ channels make Na+ permeability many times greater than K+ permeability, so Vm heads toward the Na+ equilibrium potential near +60 mV. The pump does not reverse; it moves far too few ions per millisecond to matter anyway. Concentrations barely change during a single action potential, since only a tiny number of ions have to cross to swing the voltage. Even with every K+ channel shut, the potential would still need an inward current to become positive.

cards.q: After a single action potential, what restores the small number of Na+ and K+ ions that crossed the membrane?
cards.a: The Na+/K+ ATPase, working over time rather than during the action potential.
options: The Na+/K+ ATPase, working over time rather than during the action potential
The voltage gated channels, which run backward during afterhyperpolarization
Leak channels, which carry each ion back down its concentration gradient
Nothing, because no net ion movement occurs during an action potential
cards.explanation: Each action potential moves only a tiny fraction of the cell's ions, and the Na+/K+ ATPase steadily exports the Na+ that entered and reclaims the K+ that left, so the gradients are maintained across thousands of action potentials. Voltage gated channels never run backward; they open, close, and inactivate, and ions through them always move down their electrochemical gradients. Leak channels move ions down gradients, which would degrade the gradients rather than rebuild them. There is a real, if small, net movement of ions in each action potential, which is why a pump is needed at all.

cards.q: What does the overshoot phase of the action potential mean about the membrane?
cards.a: The inside of the cell is briefly positive relative to the outside.
options: The membrane potential has become more negative than the resting value
The inside of the cell is briefly positive relative to the outside
The Na+ concentration inside has briefly exceeded that outside
The membrane potential has reached the K+ equilibrium potential
cards.explanation: Overshoot names the part of the trace above 0 mV, where so much Na+ has entered that the inside of the cell carries a net positive charge relative to the outside, reversing the usual polarity. Becoming more negative than rest is afterhyperpolarization, which is at the other end of the trace. Concentrations are essentially unchanged, because a swing of 100 mV requires only a minuscule number of ions to cross. Reaching the K+ equilibrium potential would mean about -90 mV, which is as far from overshoot as the trace ever gets.

cards.q: A mutation makes voltage gated K+ channels close faster than normal after repolarization. What happens to the trace?
cards.a: The afterhyperpolarization is reduced or absent.
options: The peak of the action potential is higher
The afterhyperpolarization is reduced or absent
The upstroke takes longer to reach threshold
The resting potential settles closer to -90 mV
cards.explanation: Afterhyperpolarization exists only because K+ channels linger open past the point where the membrane has returned to rest, so closing them promptly removes the extra K+ efflux and the trace stops at rest instead of dipping below it. The peak is determined by Na+ entry before these channels matter much, so it is unaffected. The time to reach threshold depends on the stimulus and on the graded potential, not on how K+ channels close. A resting potential nearer -90 mV would require more K+ permeability at rest, not less.

cards.q: Depolarization opens Na+ channels, and the Na+ that enters depolarizes the membrane further. What kind of control loop is this?
cards.a: Positive feedback.
options: Negative feedback
Positive feedback
Feedforward control
Tonic control
cards.explanation: The output of the process, depolarization, drives more of the same process, so the response accelerates away from the starting point until it is stopped by Na+ channel inactivation, which is the signature of positive feedback. Negative feedback opposes the change that started it, which is what the delayed K+ current does during repolarization. Feedforward control anticipates a disturbance before it happens, which is not what is going on here. Tonic control refers to a signal that is always present and varies up or down, such as sympathetic tone.

cards.q: A recorded action potential has a normal upstroke and a normal peak, but repolarization takes three times as long as usual and there is no afterhyperpolarization. Which channel is affected?
cards.a: The voltage gated K+ channel.
options: The voltage gated Na+ channel
The K+ leak channel
The voltage gated K+ channel
The chemically gated Na+ channel
cards.explanation: A normal upstroke says the Na+ channels are working, and slow repolarization with no afterhyperpolarization points straight at the outward current that normally ends the action potential, the voltage gated K+ channel. If Na+ channels were affected, the upstroke and peak would be the first things to change. Leak channels set the resting potential and would show up as a shifted baseline rather than a stretched repolarization. Chemically gated channels act at synapses and do not shape the axonal waveform at all.

cards.q: A toxin binds voltage gated Na+ channels and prevents the inactivation gate from closing, leaving activation normal. Predict the effect on the action potential.
cards.a: Depolarization is prolonged because Na+ entry continues past the normal peak.
options: No action potential occurs, because the channel can no longer open
Repolarization is faster, because the K+ current now acts unopposed
The action potential is normal but the resting potential is more negative
Depolarization is prolonged because Na+ entry continues past the normal peak
cards.explanation: Inactivation is what shuts off the inward current, so a channel that cannot inactivate keeps letting Na+ in while the K+ current is trying to repolarize, and the trace holds near the peak in a prolonged plateau before finally falling. The channel still opens normally, so an action potential does occur; it simply does not end on time. The resting potential is set mostly by K+ and by leak, not by whether Na+ inactivation works. Repolarization is slower rather than faster, because the K+ current is now working against a persistent inward Na+ current instead of an absent one.

cards.q: An axon bathed in a solution that holds its resting potential at -50 mV instead of -70 mV fires action potentials with a lower peak than normal. What explains the smaller peak?
cards.a: Sustained depolarization has left a fraction of Na+ channels inactivated.
options: Sustained depolarization has left a fraction of Na+ channels inactivated
The Na+ equilibrium potential has fallen because of the new solution
The K+ channels now open before threshold is reached
Threshold has moved to a more positive value than before
cards.explanation: Inactivation gates close in response to depolarization and only reopen when the membrane repolarizes, so a cell held at -50 mV has a standing fraction of its Na+ channels already inactivated and fewer available to carry the upstroke, giving a smaller inward current and a lower peak. The Na+ equilibrium potential depends on the Na+ concentrations, which the question does not change. K+ channels are gated by voltage but their opening is delayed and does not precede threshold. A more positive threshold would make firing harder rather than shrinking the peak of the action potentials that do occur.

cards.q: Extracellular Na+ is reduced from 145 to about 70 mEq/L. Predict the effect on the resting potential and on the action potential peak.
cards.a: Resting potential barely changes, but the peak is noticeably lower.
options: Both the resting potential and the peak become much more negative
Resting potential becomes more positive, but the peak is unchanged
Resting potential barely changes, but the peak is noticeably lower
Neither changes, because the Na+/K+ ATPase corrects the gradient
cards.explanation: At rest the membrane is dominated by K+ permeability, so cutting extracellular Na+ has only a small effect on the baseline, but the peak depends on how far the potential can climb toward the Na+ equilibrium potential, and halving extracellular Na+ makes that target substantially less positive, so the peak falls. Making both values much more negative would require a change in the K+ gradient, not the Na+ gradient. The resting potential moving positive is the wrong direction, since less external Na+ means less inward leak. The pump cannot correct a change imposed on the bathing solution; it can only move ions across the membrane.

cards.q: What does threshold represent at the trigger zone?
cards.a: The membrane potential at which inward Na+ current first exceeds outward K+ current.
options: The membrane potential at which inward Na+ current first exceeds outward K+ current
The membrane potential at which the Na+/K+ ATPase stops working
The membrane potential at which K+ channels finish closing
The membrane potential at which the peak of the action potential is finally set
cards.explanation: Threshold is a tipping point: below it, K+ leaving keeps pace with Na+ entering and the membrane drifts back to rest, and above it Na+ entry wins, opens more Na+ channels, and the positive feedback loop runs to completion. The Na+/K+ ATPase runs continuously and has no threshold behavior. K+ channel closing happens at the end of the action potential, long after threshold has been crossed. The peak is determined by Na+ entry and the Na+ equilibrium potential and is independent of where threshold sits.

cards.q: What is the typical threshold potential for a neuron?
cards.a: About -55 mV.
options: About -90 mV
About -55 mV
About -70 mV
About -30 mV
cards.explanation: Threshold sits near -55 mV, roughly 15 mV of depolarization above the usual resting potential, and reaching it commits the cell to an action potential. About -70 mV is the resting potential, the starting point rather than the tipping point. About -90 mV is the K+ equilibrium potential, approached during afterhyperpolarization. About -30 mV is well past threshold, on the rising phase of an action potential that has already been triggered.

cards.q: Where is the trigger zone in a typical multipolar neuron?
cards.a: At the axon hillock and initial segment.
options: At the axon terminal near the synaptic vesicles
At the tips of the dendrites
At the first node of Ranvier beyond the myelin
At the axon hillock and initial segment
cards.explanation: The axon hillock and the initial segment just beyond it form the trigger zone, the first stretch of membrane where the summed graded potentials are tested against threshold. Dendritic tips receive input and generate graded potentials but lack the channel density to start an action potential. Nodes of Ranvier regenerate an action potential that already exists rather than initiating one. The axon terminal is where the action potential ends and triggers transmitter release.

cards.q: What property of the trigger zone membrane makes it the site where action potentials begin?
cards.a: It has the highest density of voltage gated Na+ channels in the neuron.
options: It has the highest density of voltage gated Na+ channels in the neuron
It has the thinnest membrane in the neuron
It has the fewest leak channels found in any part of the whole neuron
It has the largest diameter of any part of the neuron
cards.explanation: Voltage gated Na+ channels are packed most densely at the axon hillock and initial segment, so a given depolarization recruits more inward current there than anywhere else and threshold is reached there first. Membrane thickness is essentially uniform across a cell and has nothing to do with it. Leak channel density affects the resting potential and passive spread but is not what defines the trigger zone. The hillock is actually a narrowing between soma and axon, so large diameter is not the explanation either.

cards.q: What does the all or none principle state about the action potential?
cards.a: Once threshold is reached, the action potential runs to full amplitude every time.
options: Every stimulus produces an action potential proportional to its strength
Once threshold is reached, the action potential runs to full amplitude every time
An action potential occurs only if every Na+ channel in the axon opens
An action potential either travels the whole axon or fails at the first node
cards.explanation: Either the depolarization reaches threshold and the positive feedback loop produces a full sized action potential, or it does not and no action potential occurs; there is no partial action potential. A response proportional to stimulus strength describes the graded potential, which is the other half of the pair students most often collapse. The principle says nothing about needing every channel to open, only about the response being complete once it starts. Conduction failure at a node is a separate phenomenon seen in demyelination and is not what the principle means.

cards.q: What is the result of a subthreshold stimulus at the trigger zone?
cards.a: A graded depolarization that decays without producing an action potential.
options: A small action potential with reduced amplitude
An action potential delayed until the stimulus is repeated
A graded depolarization that decays without producing an action potential
A hyperpolarization that moves the membrane well away from threshold
cards.explanation: A stimulus that fails to reach threshold still opens some channels and still depolarizes the membrane, but the depolarization decays passively and no positive feedback loop starts. A small action potential is precisely what the all or none principle rules out; there is no partial version. Nothing is stored and released later, so a delayed action potential from a single subthreshold stimulus does not happen, although a second stimulus arriving soon enough could summate with the first. A depolarizing stimulus moves the membrane toward threshold, not away from it.

cards.q: What is happening to the currents across the membrane exactly at threshold?
cards.a: Inward Na+ current has just become larger than outward K+ current.
options: Outward K+ current has just become larger than inward Na+ current
Inward Na+ current has just become larger than outward K+ current
Both currents have fallen to zero at the same moment
Inward Cl- current has just balanced the outward Na+ current
cards.explanation: Threshold is defined by the crossover point of the two currents: below it, K+ leaving the cell can still cancel the Na+ coming in, and above it Na+ entry outruns K+ exit and drives the membrane into the regenerative upstroke. The reverse crossover, K+ current overtaking Na+ current, is what happens at the peak and starts repolarization. Both currents at zero would describe a membrane with no permeability at all, which does not occur. Cl- carries no significant current during the initiation of an action potential in a typical axon.

cards.q: An axon is given a stimulus twice as strong as the one that just barely reached threshold. What is the amplitude of the resulting action potential?
cards.a: The same as before.
options: Twice as large as before
The same as before
Slightly larger than before
Half as large as before
cards.explanation: Amplitude is set by the ion gradients and by how many voltage gated channels the membrane has, and both are properties of the axon rather than of the stimulus, so every action potential in a given axon reaches the same peak. A doubled or slightly larger response would mean the action potential was graded, which is exactly what all or none denies. A smaller response would require fewer available Na+ channels, which a stronger stimulus does not cause. What a stronger stimulus does change is how often action potentials fire.

cards.q: A sensory axon is stimulated at three times threshold strength instead of once. What changes in its output?
cards.a: It fires more action potentials per second, each the same size.
options: It fires larger action potentials at the same rate
It fires action potentials with a longer duration each
It fires action potentials that travel faster along the axon
It fires more action potentials per second, each the same size
cards.explanation: A stronger stimulus produces a larger graded potential at the trigger zone, which drives the membrane back to threshold sooner after each action potential, so the firing rate rises while every individual action potential stays the same size. Larger action potentials would violate the all or none principle. Conduction velocity is set by axon diameter and myelination, which a stronger stimulus does not change. Duration is determined by the kinetics of the Na+ and K+ channels and is likewise fixed for a given axon.

cards.q: A neuron rests at -70 mV with a threshold of -55 mV. A stimulus produces a 10 mV depolarization at the trigger zone. What happens?
cards.a: No action potential, because the membrane reaches only -60 mV.
options: An action potential fires, because 10 mV is a large depolarization
An action potential of reduced amplitude fires
No action potential, because the membrane reaches only -60 mV
No action potential, and the membrane potential does not change at all
cards.explanation: Threshold is 15 mV of depolarization away from rest, so a 10 mV depolarization brings the membrane to -60 mV and stops 5 mV short, and the potential decays back toward rest. Judging the stimulus by its size in millivolts without comparing it to the gap between rest and threshold is the common error here. A reduced amplitude action potential is not possible under the all or none principle. The membrane potential does change, from -70 to -60 mV, which is a real graded potential even though it fails to trigger anything.

cards.q: Two subthreshold stimuli summate at the trigger zone and together cross threshold. What is the resulting action potential like?
cards.a: Full sized, identical to one produced by a single strong stimulus.
options: Full sized, identical to one produced by a single strong stimulus
Half sized, because each stimulus contributed half of the depolarization
Larger than usual, because two stimuli contributed to it
Delayed but smaller, because threshold was reached gradually
cards.explanation: Once threshold is crossed, the positive feedback loop between depolarization and Na+ channel opening runs the same way no matter how the membrane got there, so the action potential is full sized. Splitting the amplitude between the two stimuli treats the action potential as if it were graded. Adding the stimuli together to make a bigger action potential makes the same mistake in the other direction. How slowly threshold is approached can affect the timing and, through accommodation, whether firing happens at all, but it does not scale the amplitude of an action potential that does occur.

cards.q: A drug shifts a neuron's threshold from -55 mV to -45 mV without changing the resting potential. How does the neuron's excitability change?
cards.a: It becomes less excitable, since a larger depolarization is now needed.
options: It becomes more excitable, since threshold is now closer to the peak
It is unchanged, because the resting potential did not move
It becomes less excitable, since a larger depolarization is now needed
It becomes less excitable, because the action potential amplitude falls
cards.explanation: Excitability depends on the gap between rest and threshold, and that gap has grown from 15 mV to 25 mV, so inputs that used to fire the cell now fall short. Proximity to the peak is irrelevant, since the peak is a consequence of firing rather than a target the membrane has to reach. Holding the resting potential constant does not protect excitability when the other end of the gap moves. Amplitude is set by the ion gradients and does not fall just because threshold shifted.

cards.q: Which of these changes will alter the amplitude of the action potentials recorded from a single axon?
cards.a: A large drop in extracellular Na+ concentration.
options: A doubling of stimulus intensity
A longer duration of the applied stimulus
An increase in the frequency of stimulation within the axon's limits
A large drop in extracellular Na+ concentration
cards.explanation: Amplitude depends on how far the membrane can move toward the Na+ equilibrium potential, so cutting extracellular Na+ lowers that target and shrinks the action potential. Stimulus intensity, stimulus duration, and firing frequency are all properties of the input, and the all or none principle means none of them scales the response as long as threshold is reached. Frequency can reduce amplitude if it is pushed into the relative refractory period, but within the axon's normal limits it does not.

cards.q: A neuron is hyperpolarized from -70 mV to -80 mV by an inhibitory input. What size depolarization is now needed to reach a threshold of -55 mV?
cards.a: 25 mV, up from the usual 15 mV.
options: 10 mV, less than before
15 mV, the same as before
80 mV, the full distance from zero
25 mV, up from the usual 15 mV
cards.explanation: The membrane now sits 25 mV below threshold instead of 15 mV, so a larger depolarization is required and the same synaptic input that used to fire the cell may no longer do so. Fifteen millivolts would be the answer only if the resting potential were still -70 mV. Needing less depolarization would be true of a cell depolarized toward threshold, not hyperpolarized away from it. Measuring from zero misreads the scale; what matters is the distance from the current potential to threshold.

cards.q: A recorded response grows from 5 mV to 12 mV when the stimulus is doubled, and it never overshoots zero. What kind of response is it?
cards.a: A graded potential.
options: An action potential recorded near its origin
A graded potential
An action potential with partial Na+ channel block
An afterhyperpolarization following a subthreshold stimulus
cards.explanation: Scaling with stimulus strength is the defining behavior of a graded potential, and the absence of an overshoot confirms that no regenerative Na+ current ever took over. An action potential recorded anywhere along its path is the same size, so a response that doubles cannot be one. Partial Na+ channel block does lower the peak, but the remaining action potentials would still be all or none rather than proportional to the stimulus. Afterhyperpolarization follows an action potential and is a hyperpolarization, not the depolarizing response described here.

cards.q: An axon is stimulated at two, five, and ten times threshold. The recorded action potentials are identical in height each time, but they come faster at higher intensities. What does this demonstrate?
cards.a: Amplitude is all or none, and intensity is carried by firing frequency instead.
options: Amplitude is all or none, and intensity is carried by firing frequency instead
The axon is being damaged by the stronger stimuli
The recording electrode is saturating at each of the higher stimulus strengths
Stronger stimuli recruit additional ion channels in the same axon
cards.explanation: Constant height across a fivefold range of stimulus strength is the experimental signature of all or none behavior, and the rising rate shows where the intensity information actually goes, into frequency coding. Damage would change the shape or abolish the response rather than leave it perfectly reproducible. A saturating electrode would clip the trace at some point rather than reproduce the same waveform from the weakest stimulus onward. Stronger stimuli do open more channels in the dendrites, which enlarges the graded potential, but the axon's action potential still uses the same channels to the same endpoint.

cards.q: A neuron's resting potential drifts from -70 mV to -60 mV and stays there, with threshold still at -55 mV. Predict how easily it fires and why the prediction is not simply that it fires more easily.
cards.a: It fires more easily at first, then fails as sustained depolarization inactivates Na+ channels.
options: It fires more easily, and this continues indefinitely as the gap to threshold keeps shrinking
It fires less easily, because the depolarization has raised the threshold voltage
It fires more easily at first, then fails as sustained depolarization inactivates Na+ channels
Its firing is unchanged, because the threshold voltage itself has not moved at all
cards.explanation: Two effects run in opposite directions: the gap from rest to threshold has shrunk from 15 mV to 5 mV, which makes firing easier, but a membrane held depolarized keeps a growing fraction of Na+ channels in the inactivated state, which reduces the current available and eventually blocks firing altogether. Treating only the first effect as the whole answer is the common half learned version. Threshold itself has not moved further away; the resting potential moved toward it. Saying nothing changes ignores the shortened gap that clearly does matter.

cards.q: A neuron receives a large EPSP that clearly depolarizes the trigger zone past -55 mV, yet no action potential occurs. A toxin is present. What has the toxin most likely done?
cards.a: Blocked a large fraction of the voltage gated Na+ channels at the trigger zone.
options: Blocked the Na+/K+ ATPase in the cell body and along the axon
Blocked the voltage gated K+ channels along the whole length of the axon
Blocked a large fraction of the voltage gated Na+ channels at the trigger zone
Blocked the chemically gated channels on the dendrites and cell body
cards.explanation: Reaching -55 mV only fires the cell if enough Na+ channels are available to make the inward current outrun the outward one, so removing most of those channels raises the true threshold above the potential reached and the depolarization simply decays. Blocking K+ channels would prolong an action potential rather than prevent one. Blocking the pump degrades gradients over minutes and would not abolish firing this abruptly. Blocking dendritic chemically gated channels would prevent the EPSP, but the question states that a large EPSP occurred.

cards.q: Extracellular Ca2+ falls well below normal, and voltage gated Na+ channels in this state begin to open at more negative membrane potentials than usual. Predict the effect on the neuron.
cards.a: It becomes hyperexcitable, firing in response to inputs that were previously subthreshold.
options: It becomes hyperexcitable, firing in response to inputs that were previously subthreshold
It becomes less excitable, because Ca2+ normally carries the upstroke
It is unchanged, because Ca2+ acts only at the axon terminal
Its action potentials become much larger, because more Na+ channels now open at once
cards.explanation: Extracellular Ca2+ normally sits at the outer face of the membrane and makes the Na+ channels behave as if the membrane were more polarized than it is, so losing it shifts channel opening to more negative potentials, effectively lowering threshold and letting ordinary inputs trigger firing. Ca2+ does not carry the neuronal upstroke; Na+ does, so the loss is not a loss of inward charge carrier. Ca2+ entry at the terminal does drive transmitter release, but the membrane surface effect described here acts along the whole neuron. Amplitude stays all or none because the Na+ gradient and channel population are unchanged.

cards.q: In a single sensory axon, what feature of the action potential train carries information about stimulus strength?
cards.a: The number of action potentials per second.
options: The number of action potentials per second
The height of each action potential
The conduction velocity of each action potential
The duration of each action potential
cards.explanation: Because every action potential in an axon is the same size, the only thing left to vary is how often they occur, so the nervous system reads stimulus strength from firing frequency. Height is fixed by the ion gradients and the all or none principle. Conduction velocity is a fixed property of the axon set by diameter and myelination, so it cannot vary with the stimulus. Duration is set by channel kinetics and stays essentially constant from one action potential to the next.

cards.q: What is frequency coding?
cards.a: Representing stimulus intensity by the rate of action potential firing.
options: Representing stimulus intensity by the rate of action potential firing
Representing stimulus type by the rate of action potential firing
Representing stimulus intensity by the size of each action potential
Representing stimulus location by the speed of conduction
cards.explanation: Frequency coding is the strategy of letting the interval between action potentials carry the intensity information, since the action potentials themselves are all identical. Stimulus type, or modality, is carried instead by which pathway the signal travels, the labeled line principle. Coding intensity by action potential size is exactly what the all or none principle rules out. Conduction velocity differs between fiber types but is a fixed axon property and does not encode location.

cards.q: What is population coding, also called recruitment, in a sensory pathway?
cards.a: Representing a stronger stimulus by activating a larger number of sensory neurons.
options: Representing a stronger stimulus by activating a larger number of sensory neurons
Representing a stronger stimulus by lengthening each action potential
Representing a stronger stimulus by increasing conduction velocity in the active axons
Representing a stronger stimulus by widening the receptive field of one neuron
cards.explanation: Sensory neurons differ in threshold, so a weak stimulus activates only the most sensitive ones and a strong stimulus brings additional, less sensitive neurons into the response, and the brain reads the size of the active population as part of the intensity signal. Action potential duration and conduction velocity are fixed properties of a given axon and do not scale with stimulus strength. A neuron's receptive field is anatomically determined and does not expand with a stronger stimulus, although more of it may be stimulated.

cards.q: Does the amplitude of an action potential carry information about how strong the stimulus was?
cards.a: No, because amplitude is all or none and fixed for a given axon.
options: Yes, larger stimuli produce proportionally larger action potentials
No, because amplitude is all or none and fixed for a given axon
Yes, but only in unmyelinated axons
No, because amplitude varies randomly from one action potential to the next
cards.explanation: Once threshold is crossed, the same ion gradients and the same channel population drive every action potential to the same peak, so amplitude carries no intensity information and the nervous system must encode strength some other way. Proportional amplitude describes the graded potential that starts the process, not the action potential that results. Myelination changes speed, not amplitude, so the exception offered does not exist. Amplitude is highly reproducible rather than random, which is why frequency is a reliable code by comparison.

cards.q: Which electrical signal in a sensory neuron does vary in amplitude with stimulus strength?
cards.a: The receptor potential at the sensory ending.
options: The action potential at the first node of Ranvier
The resting membrane potential of the axon
The afterhyperpolarization following each action potential
The receptor potential at the sensory ending
cards.explanation: The receptor potential is a graded potential produced by mechanically or chemically gated channels at the sensory ending, and a stronger stimulus opens more of them and makes it larger, which is where the intensity information enters the system. Action potentials at any point along the axon are all or none and identical. Afterhyperpolarization is a fixed consequence of K+ channel kinetics rather than a signal that scales with the stimulus. The resting potential is a baseline, not a response.

cards.q: What sets the upper limit on how fast a neuron can fire action potentials?
cards.a: The refractory period.
options: The speed of the Na+/K+ ATPase
The conduction velocity of the axon
The refractory period
The size of the receptor potential
cards.explanation: After each action potential the membrane cannot fire again until Na+ channels recover from inactivation, so the refractory period sets the shortest possible interval between action potentials and therefore the maximum frequency. The Na+/K+ ATPase restores gradients over a much longer timescale and is not the limiting step between successive action potentials. Conduction velocity determines how fast a signal travels, not how often one can be launched. A larger receptor potential pushes the firing rate up, but the ceiling it runs into is refractoriness.

cards.q: What is meant by recruitment in a sensory response?
cards.a: Bringing additional sensory neurons into the response as stimulus strength rises.
options: Bringing additional Na+ channels into the action potential in one axon
Bringing additional sensory neurons into the response as stimulus strength rises
Bringing additional neurotransmitter into the synapse at higher frequencies
Bringing additional myelin onto an axon during repeated use
cards.explanation: Sensory neurons vary in threshold, and recruitment names the progressive activation of the higher threshold ones as the stimulus grows, adding to the total signal reaching the brain. More Na+ channels opening within one axon happens during every action potential and is not what the term describes. Increased transmitter release does accompany higher firing rates, but that is synaptic facilitation of output rather than recruitment of neurons. Myelin is laid down during development and is not added in response to a stimulus.

cards.q: A single sensory axon's firing rate stops rising once a stimulus becomes very intense. What is this limit called?
cards.a: Saturation of the frequency code.
options: Adaptation of the receptor
Accommodation of the trigger zone
Habituation of the pathway
Saturation of the frequency code
cards.explanation: Saturation is the ceiling imposed by the refractory period: once action potentials are packed as closely as the membrane allows, further increases in stimulus strength cannot raise the rate, and that axon can no longer report the difference. Adaptation is a fall in firing rate during a maintained stimulus, which is a decline rather than a ceiling. Accommodation is the failure to fire when depolarization arrives too slowly, because Na+ channels inactivate on the way up. Habituation is a reduction in a behavioral response with repetition and is a property of circuits rather than of one axon.

cards.q: Pressure on a receptor doubles, and its axon goes from firing 10 action potentials per second to 25 per second while each spike stays the same height. What does this illustrate?
cards.a: Frequency coding of stimulus intensity.
options: Frequency coding of stimulus intensity
Amplitude coding of stimulus intensity
Recruitment of additional sensory neurons
Adaptation of the receptor to a sustained stimulus
cards.explanation: Identical spike heights with a rising rate is exactly what frequency coding looks like: the intensity information is in the intervals, not in the spikes. Amplitude coding would require the spikes to grow, which the all or none principle forbids. Recruitment involves more neurons joining in and cannot be seen in a recording from a single axon. Adaptation is a fall in firing rate during a maintained stimulus, the opposite of the increase described here.

cards.q: A light touch activates three axons from a skin region, while firm pressure at the same spot activates twenty. What mechanism does this show?
cards.a: Recruitment of higher threshold receptors as the stimulus grows.
options: Frequency coding within a single axon
Recruitment of higher threshold receptors as the stimulus grows
Temporal summation of graded potentials arriving at one dendrite
Saltatory conduction spreading to neighboring axons
cards.explanation: Different receptors have different thresholds, so a stronger stimulus crosses more of those thresholds and brings additional axons into the response, giving the brain a larger active population to read as greater intensity. Frequency coding is about the rate within one axon and cannot explain a change in how many axons are active. Temporal summation happens inside one neuron and does not activate other neurons. Saltatory conduction is how a signal moves along one myelinated axon, and action potentials do not jump between separate axons.

cards.q: An axon has an absolute refractory period of 2 ms. What is its approximate maximum firing frequency?
cards.a: About 500 action potentials per second.
options: About 50 action potentials per second
About 200 action potentials per second
About 500 action potentials per second
About 2000 action potentials per second
cards.explanation: If no action potential can start until 2 ms after the last one, the shortest possible interval is 2 ms and the ceiling is one divided by 0.002 seconds, which is 500 per second. Fifty per second would correspond to a 20 ms refractory period. Two hundred per second corresponds to 5 ms. Two thousand per second would require a 0.5 ms refractory period, which is far shorter than any real axon achieves.

cards.q: Which feature of a sensory signal tells the brain what kind of stimulus occurred rather than how strong it was?
cards.a: Which pathway the action potentials arrive on.
options: How many action potentials arrive per second
Which pathway the action potentials arrive on
How tall the arriving action potentials are
How fast the action potentials conducted
cards.explanation: Modality is carried by the labeled line: the brain interprets activity in the optic pathway as light and activity in a pain pathway as pain, regardless of what actually stimulated the receptor. Firing rate is the intensity code and says how much, not what kind. Action potential height is constant and carries no information at all. Conduction velocity varies between fiber types and affects timing, but the identity of the sensation comes from the destination of the pathway.

cards.q: A recording shows spikes of identical height that are spaced 20 ms apart during a weak stimulus and 5 ms apart during a strong one. What is the firing rate in each case?
cards.a: 50 per second when weak and 200 per second when strong.
options: 20 per second when weak and 5 per second when strong
5 per second when weak and 20 per second when strong
50 per second when weak and 200 per second when strong
200 per second when weak and 50 per second when strong
cards.explanation: Rate is the reciprocal of the interval, so a 20 ms gap gives 1 divided by 0.020 seconds, or 50 per second, and a 5 ms gap gives 200 per second. Reading the interval in milliseconds directly as a rate skips the conversion and gets it backward. Reversing the two values would mean the strong stimulus fired more slowly, which contradicts the shorter interval. The identical spike heights confirm that all the information here lives in the timing.

cards.q: A synapse produces a larger graded potential at the trigger zone than it did before. What happens to the postsynaptic neuron's output?
cards.a: It fires action potentials at a higher frequency.
options: It fires action potentials that conduct faster down the axon
It fires action potentials with a larger amplitude
It fires action potentials at a higher frequency
It fires the same number of action potentials but with less delay each
cards.explanation: A larger depolarization at the trigger zone drives the membrane back up to threshold sooner after each refractory period ends, so action potentials come closer together and the firing rate rises. Amplitude cannot change, since the action potential is all or none. Conduction velocity depends on axon diameter and myelination, neither of which the synapse alters. Latency to the first action potential does shorten, but the sustained response is a change in rate, not merely in the timing of a fixed number of spikes.

cards.q: Why can the nervous system not use action potential amplitude to signal a very intense stimulus?
cards.a: Because action potentials are all or none and always reach the same peak in a given axon.
options: Because amplitude is used to signal stimulus modality instead
Because action potentials are all or none and always reach the same peak in a given axon
Because the sensory pathways cannot resolve such small differences in spike height reliably
Because amplitude falls as the action potential travels down the axon
cards.explanation: Once threshold is reached the regenerative Na+ current takes the membrane to the same peak every time, set by the ion gradients rather than by the stimulus, so amplitude is a constant and constants cannot carry information. Modality is signaled by which pathway is active, not by spike height. There is no measurement problem to blame; the amplitudes really are the same. Amplitude falling with distance describes a graded potential, and it is precisely because action potentials do not decay that they can carry a signal over a long axon.

cards.q: A weak touch produces 5 action potentials per second in 3 axons. A firm press produces 40 per second in 20 axons. Which two coding mechanisms are at work?
cards.a: Frequency coding within each axon and population coding across axons.
options: Amplitude coding within each axon and frequency coding across axons
Temporal summation within each axon and spatial summation across axons
Population coding within each axon and labeled line coding across axons
Frequency coding within each axon and population coding across axons
cards.explanation: Two things changed at once: each active axon raised its rate eightfold, which is frequency coding, and the number of active axons rose from 3 to 20, which is recruitment or population coding, and together they give the brain a much larger total signal. Amplitude coding is ruled out because action potentials do not vary in size. Population coding is by definition a property of a group and cannot occur within a single axon. Temporal and spatial summation describe how graded potentials add inside one neuron, not how a population reports intensity.

cards.q: A toxin lengthens an axon's absolute refractory period from 1 ms to 4 ms. Predict the effect on how the axon reports a very intense stimulus.
cards.a: Its maximum rate falls from about 1000 to about 250 per second, saturating the code.
options: Its conduction velocity falls fourfold, so intense stimuli arrive a second late
Its action potentials become four times smaller, so intense stimuli signal weakly
Its maximum rate falls from about 1000 to about 250 per second, saturating the code
Its threshold rises fourfold, so weak and moderate stimuli go undetected
cards.explanation: Maximum frequency is the reciprocal of the refractory period, so it drops from about 1000 to about 250 per second, and once the axon is firing at that ceiling any further increase in stimulus strength cannot raise the rate, which means strong and very strong stimuli become indistinguishable. Amplitude is set by ion gradients and channel availability, not by refractory duration. Conduction velocity depends on diameter and myelination and is a separate property. Threshold is about how much depolarization starts an action potential and is not what a longer refractory period changes.

cards.q: A subject reports that a stimulus feels stronger, but a recording from one sensory axon shows no change in its firing rate. What most likely accounts for the stronger sensation?
cards.a: Additional sensory neurons with higher thresholds have been recruited.
options: The action potentials in the recorded axon have grown taller than before
The recorded axon is conducting more rapidly than before
The refractory period in the recorded axon has shortened
Additional sensory neurons with higher thresholds have been recruited
cards.explanation: If the one axon being watched is unchanged, the extra signal has to come from elsewhere, and the standard mechanism is recruitment of less sensitive receptors and their axons, which enlarges the active population. Taller action potentials would violate the all or none principle and would not be a code the brain reads anyway. Faster conduction would change arrival time rather than perceived strength. A shortened refractory period would raise the maximum possible rate, but the question states the actual rate did not change.

cards.q: A constant pressure is applied to the skin. The receptor potential decays over several seconds and the axon's firing rate falls with it, even though the pressure has not changed. What does this tell you about the intensity code?
cards.a: Firing rate tracks the receptor potential, so it reports change in the stimulus rather than only its absolute strength.
options: Firing rate tracks the receptor potential, so it reports change in the stimulus rather than only its absolute strength
Firing rate is independent of the receptor potential, so the decline must come from damage to the axon Na+ channels
Firing rate has reached the ceiling set by the refractory period
Firing rate has fallen because the action potentials have become smaller
cards.explanation: The firing rate is generated by whatever depolarization the trigger zone receives, so as the receptor potential adapts and shrinks, the rate falls with it, and the code ends up emphasizing changes in stimulation over steady background. Attributing the decline to channel damage misses that the receptor potential itself was observed to decay, which is the upstream cause. A refractory ceiling would show up as a rate that stops rising, not one that falls during an unchanging stimulus. Action potential size does not vary, so it cannot explain a falling rate.

cards.q: What is the absolute refractory period?
cards.a: The interval during which no stimulus, however strong, can trigger another action potential.
options: The interval during which a stronger than normal stimulus can still trigger an action potential
The interval during which the membrane is more negative than the resting potential
The interval during which no stimulus, however strong, can trigger another action potential
The interval during which the Na+/K+ ATPase restores the ion gradients
cards.explanation: During the absolute refractory period the voltage gated Na+ channels are inactivated, and since inactivation gates reopen only after repolarization, no amount of depolarizing current can produce another action potential. The interval where a stronger stimulus still works is the relative refractory period, which follows the absolute one. Being more negative than rest describes afterhyperpolarization, which overlaps the relative period rather than defining the absolute one. Restoring gradients by pump activity takes far longer and is not what limits firing between two action potentials.

cards.q: What is the relative refractory period?
cards.a: The interval during which a stronger than normal stimulus can trigger an action potential.
options: The interval during which no stimulus can trigger an action potential
The interval during which the action potential is still traveling along the axon and its branches
The interval during which a stronger than normal stimulus can trigger an action potential
The interval during which the membrane potential is above threshold
cards.explanation: In the relative refractory period some Na+ channels have recovered from inactivation while K+ channels are still open, so firing is possible but requires extra depolarization to overcome the lingering outward current. An interval where nothing works is the absolute refractory period. The travel of an action potential down the axon happens regardless and is not a refractory state. A membrane above threshold is in the middle of an action potential, not in a recovery period.

cards.q: What is the state of the voltage gated Na+ channels during the absolute refractory period?
cards.a: Inactivated, with the inactivation gate closed.
options: Blocked by extracellular Ca2+ binding to the pore
Resting, with the activation gate closed and the inactivation gate open
Open, with both gates open
Inactivated, with the inactivation gate closed
cards.explanation: Inactivation gates swing shut shortly after the channels open and stay shut until the membrane repolarizes, so the channels are physically unavailable and this unavailability is exactly what makes the period absolute. The resting configuration is the ready state the channel returns to once repolarization is complete, which ends the absolute period. Both gates open is the conducting state during the upstroke. Extracellular Ca2+ influences the voltage at which channels open but does not plug the pore in this way.

cards.q: What channel states define the relative refractory period?
cards.a: Some Na+ channels have recovered while many voltage gated K+ channels are still open.
options: All Na+ channels are still inactivated and the K+ channels have already closed
All Na+ channels have recovered and all the voltage gated K+ channels have closed
Some Na+ channels have recovered while many voltage gated K+ channels are still open
Na+ channels are open and the voltage gated K+ channels are inactivated
cards.explanation: Two things are true at once in the relative period: a growing fraction of Na+ channels has returned to the resting, ready configuration, and the slow K+ channels have not yet shut, so the outward current is still opposing any new depolarization and a larger stimulus is needed. All Na+ channels inactivated with K+ channels closed does not describe any single moment of the action potential. Full recovery with K+ channels closed is simply the resting state, where excitability is normal. Voltage gated K+ channels do not inactivate the way Na+ channels do.

cards.q: When does the absolute refractory period begin?
cards.a: At threshold, when the voltage gated Na+ channels open.
options: At threshold, when the voltage gated Na+ channels open
At the peak of the action potential
At the start of afterhyperpolarization
When the membrane potential has returned all the way to rest
cards.explanation: From the moment the Na+ channels open at threshold, a second action potential cannot be started in that patch of membrane, so the absolute period covers the whole upstroke and most of repolarization. Starting the clock at the peak would leave the entire rising phase unaccounted for, and a second action potential cannot be launched then either. Afterhyperpolarization marks roughly the relative period, which comes later. The return to rest is where refractoriness is ending, not beginning.

cards.q: Which part of the action potential trace corresponds roughly to the relative refractory period?
cards.a: The afterhyperpolarization.
options: The rising phase to the peak
The overshoot above 0 mV
The flat baseline before the stimulus
The afterhyperpolarization
cards.explanation: Afterhyperpolarization occurs while K+ channels remain open and Na+ channels are still recovering, which is the same condition that defines the relative refractory period, so the two overlap closely. The rising phase and the overshoot both fall inside the absolute refractory period, when nothing can be triggered. The flat baseline before a stimulus is the fully rested membrane, which is by definition not refractory at all.

cards.q: What must happen before an inactivated Na+ channel can conduct again?
cards.a: The membrane must repolarize.
options: The Na+/K+ ATPase must complete one full cycle
The membrane must repolarize
The channel must bind a neurotransmitter
Extracellular Na+ must be restored to its normal value
cards.explanation: Inactivation gates are voltage sensitive and reopen only when the membrane potential returns toward negative values, which is why the return from inactivation tracks repolarization so closely and why the refractory period ends when it does. The Na+/K+ ATPase maintains gradients over a much longer timescale and is not required between two consecutive action potentials. These are voltage gated channels, so transmitter binding plays no part. Extracellular Na+ barely changes during an action potential, so nothing needs restoring there.

cards.q: During the relative refractory period, what kind of stimulus can still produce an action potential?
cards.a: A stimulus stronger than the one normally needed.
options: A stimulus stronger than the one normally needed
Only a stimulus applied at a different site on the axon
A stimulus of the same strength as before
A hyperpolarizing stimulus
