cards.explanation: Fewer Na+ channels are available and the K+ current is still working against depolarization, so a larger than usual inward push is needed to reach the tipping point, and that is what makes the period relative rather than absolute. Moving the stimulus to a different site tests a different patch of membrane and does not describe what this patch can do. A normal strength stimulus is exactly what fails during this window. A hyperpolarizing stimulus moves the membrane away from threshold and never initiates firing.

cards.q: An axon cannot fire again at normal stimulus strength until about 4 ms after the previous action potential. What is its maximum firing frequency?
cards.a: About 250 action potentials per second.
options: About 250 action potentials per second
About 40 action potentials per second
About 4 action potentials per second
About 400 action potentials per second
cards.explanation: The shortest usable interval is 4 ms, so the ceiling is 1 divided by 0.004 seconds, which is 250 per second. Reading 4 ms as 4 per second confuses an interval with a rate. Forty per second would correspond to a 25 ms interval, far longer than any refractory period. Four hundred per second would require a 2.5 ms interval, which is shorter than the 4 ms the question specifies.

cards.q: An action potential at the middle of an axon spreads local current in both directions. Why does it not travel backward toward the cell body?
cards.a: The membrane behind it is in its absolute refractory period.
options: Local current can only flow in the direction the axon points
The membrane behind it is in its absolute refractory period
Myelin blocks current from spreading backward
The Na+/K+ ATPase pumps the charge forward
cards.explanation: Current really does spread both ways, but the membrane just behind the action potential has inactivated Na+ channels and cannot respond, so only the membrane ahead is able to reach threshold and the signal moves in one direction. Cytoplasmic current has no built in direction; it flows wherever there is a voltage difference. Myelin insulates the internode but does not distinguish forward from backward. The pump is far too slow to influence events within a millisecond and does not push charge along the axon.

cards.q: A second stimulus is applied to an axon 1 ms after the peak of an action potential, using a current ten times normal strength. What happens?
cards.a: No action potential, because the membrane is still absolutely refractory.
options: An action potential of normal size fires
An action potential of reduced size fires
No action potential, because the membrane is still absolutely refractory
No action potential, because the stimulus is too strong and blocks the channels
cards.explanation: One millisecond after the peak the membrane is still repolarizing and most Na+ channels remain inactivated, so no stimulus of any size can produce an action potential. A normal or reduced action potential would require at least some Na+ channels to be available, which is the situation later, during the relative refractory period. Excessively strong stimuli can damage tissue, but ordinary experimental currents do not fail by blocking channels; the failure here is inactivation.

cards.q: A stimulus is applied during the afterhyperpolarization, using a current larger than the usual threshold stimulus. What is the most likely result?
cards.a: An action potential fires, possibly with a slightly reduced peak.
options: An action potential fires, possibly with a slightly reduced peak
No action potential can occur at any stimulus strength
An action potential fires with a larger than normal peak
The membrane depolarizes but stays permanently above threshold
cards.explanation: Afterhyperpolarization overlaps the relative refractory period, when enough Na+ channels have recovered for a strong stimulus to work, though with fewer channels available and a lingering K+ current the resulting action potential can be somewhat smaller. Complete failure at any strength is the absolute period, which has already ended by this point. A larger than normal peak would require more Na+ channels than usual, which is the opposite of the situation. Membranes do not lock above threshold; the K+ current always brings them back.

cards.q: A drug speeds the recovery of Na+ channels from inactivation without changing anything else. What happens to the axon's maximum firing frequency?
cards.a: It rises, because the refractory period is shorter.
options: It falls, because the action potentials become longer
It falls, because the channels spend less time in the open state
It is unchanged, because frequency is set by stimulus strength alone
It rises, because the refractory period is shorter
cards.explanation: The refractory period exists because inactivated channels take time to become available again, so accelerating that recovery shortens the interval before the next action potential can start and raises the ceiling on firing rate. Time spent open is governed by the activation and inactivation kinetics of the upstroke, not by how fast recovery happens afterward. Stimulus strength drives the rate up toward the ceiling, but the ceiling itself is set by refractoriness. Nothing here lengthens the action potential; that would require slower K+ channels.

cards.q: An experimenter stimulates an axon in the middle of its length and records from both ends. What is observed?
cards.a: Action potentials travel in both directions from the stimulus site.
options: Action potentials travel only toward the axon terminal
Action potentials travel in both directions from the stimulus site
No action potential occurs, because the trigger zone was bypassed
Action potentials travel only toward the cell body
cards.explanation: Nothing about the axon membrane is inherently one way; the direction of normal traffic is set by where the action potential starts, and a stimulus in the middle finds unrefractory membrane on both sides, so two action potentials propagate away from each other. Believing the axon can only conduct toward the terminal confuses a normal starting point with a structural rule. The trigger zone is where action potentials normally begin, but any patch of axon membrane with voltage gated Na+ channels can be excited directly. Conduction toward the cell body alone has no basis either.

cards.q: Why does an axon's firing rate stop increasing once the stimulus becomes very strong?
cards.a: The refractory period sets a ceiling on how closely action potentials can come.
options: The Na+ gradient is exhausted by the ion movement at high firing rates
Threshold rises steadily each time the stimulus intensity is increased further
The action potentials begin to shrink and eventually fail to propagate
The refractory period sets a ceiling on how closely action potentials can come
cards.explanation: A stronger stimulus can only make the membrane reach threshold sooner, and it cannot make it reach threshold before the Na+ channels have recovered, so the rate saturates at roughly the reciprocal of the refractory period. The Na+ gradient survives thousands of action potentials because so few ions cross each time, so exhaustion is not the limit. Amplitude does drop somewhat when firing intrudes into the relative refractory period, but that is a consequence rather than the reason the rate plateaus. Threshold does not climb with stimulus intensity.

cards.q: Paired stimuli are delivered to an axon. At a 1 ms interval the second stimulus gives no response, at 4 ms it gives a smaller action potential, and at 10 ms it gives a full one. What do the three intervals correspond to?
cards.a: Absolute refractory at 1 ms, relative refractory at 4 ms, and full recovery by 10 ms.
options: Relative refractory at 1 ms, absolute refractory at 4 ms, and full recovery by 10 ms
Full recovery at 1 ms, absolute refractory at 4 ms, and relative refractory at 10 ms
Absolute refractory at 1 ms, relative refractory at 4 ms, and full recovery by 10 ms
Absolute refractory at all three intervals, with the response growing as channels open
cards.explanation: No response at any strength means the Na+ channels are still inactivated, which is the absolute period, a reduced response means some have recovered while K+ channels remain open, which is the relative period, and a normal response means the membrane has returned to its resting readiness. Putting the relative period first reverses the order in which the channels recover. Full recovery cannot precede refractoriness, since the channels inactivate before they recover. If all three intervals were absolutely refractory, none of them would give a response at all.

cards.q: A toxin slows the recovery of Na+ channels from inactivation. A motor neuron is then driven at 100 action potentials per second. Predict what happens.
cards.a: The axon drops action potentials, since the interval is now shorter than the refractory period.
options: The axon fires normally, since recovery affects only the size of each individual action potential
The axon drops action potentials, since the interval is now shorter than the refractory period
The axon fires faster, since inactivated channels no longer oppose depolarization
The axon fires normally at that rate but conducts each action potential more slowly
cards.explanation: At 100 per second the intervals are 10 ms, and if recovery now takes longer than that, the membrane is still refractory when the next command arrives, so some action potentials simply never occur and the output rate falls below the input rate. Slow recovery does affect how many channels are available and hence amplitude, but the more important consequence at high rates is outright failure. Inactivated channels do not assist depolarization; they remove the current that produces it. Conduction velocity is set by cable properties and available Na+ current, and while a severe block can slow conduction, the defining problem here is a rate ceiling.

cards.q: A neuron can follow a 50 Hz drive faithfully but starts dropping action potentials at 200 Hz. What does this indicate about its refractory period?
cards.a: It is longer than 5 ms but shorter than 20 ms.
options: It is shorter than 5 ms
It is longer than 5 ms but shorter than 20 ms
It is longer than 20 ms
It cannot be estimated from firing rates
cards.explanation: Following 50 Hz means the neuron can fire at 20 ms intervals, so the refractory period is under 20 ms, and failing at 200 Hz means it cannot fire at 5 ms intervals, so the refractory period is longer than 5 ms. A period under 5 ms would have allowed the neuron to follow 200 Hz. A period over 20 ms would have caused failure at 50 Hz as well. The refractory period is precisely what the maximum following frequency measures, so it can certainly be estimated this way.

cards.q: A demyelinated axon conducts action potentials at one tenth of its normal velocity. Does the refractory period still prevent backward conduction?
cards.a: Yes, because direction depends on the channel state behind it, not on speed.
options: Yes, because direction depends on the channel state behind it, not on speed
No, because the slower signal gives the membrane behind it time to recover
No, because demyelination removes the refractory period from the axon entirely
Yes, but only when the axon is stimulated at its trigger zone rather than midway
cards.explanation: One way conduction depends on the membrane just behind the advancing action potential being inactivated when the local current reaches it, and slowing conduction does not change the fact that the region behind has just fired and is refractory. It is true that if conduction were slowed enough for the trailing membrane to fully recover, reexcitation could occur, and that is the basis of reentry in cardiac muscle, but a tenfold slowing in an axon still leaves the trailing membrane refractory. Demyelination changes insulation, not channel gating, so the refractory period itself is intact. The stimulation site determines which way the action potential starts out, not whether it can double back.

cards.q: How does a larger axon diameter affect conduction velocity?
cards.a: It increases velocity, because a wider cytoplasmic path resists current less.
options: It increases velocity, because a wider cytoplasmic path resists current less
It decreases velocity, because more membrane must be depolarized
It has no effect, since velocity depends only on myelination
It increases velocity, because larger axons carry more Na+/K+ ATPase per node
cards.explanation: A wider axon offers a lower resistance path for current flowing lengthwise, so the local current from an active patch reaches farther ahead and brings distant membrane to threshold sooner, which speeds conduction. There is more membrane to depolarize in a wide axon, but the drop in internal resistance outweighs it, which is why the giant axons of invertebrates are fast. Myelination is a second major factor, not the only one. Pump density affects long term gradient maintenance, not the speed of a single action potential.

cards.q: How does myelination affect conduction velocity?
cards.a: It increases velocity by reducing current leak across the internodal membrane.
options: It increases velocity by adding voltage gated Na+ channels along the internode
It increases velocity by reducing current leak across the internodal membrane
It decreases velocity by insulating the axon from the extracellular fluid
It increases velocity by widening the axon inside the myelin sheath
cards.explanation: Myelin wraps the internode in many layers of membrane, which raises membrane resistance so that local current stays inside the axon and travels far enough to reach the next node quickly. Voltage gated Na+ channels are concentrated at the nodes and are actually excluded from the internode, so myelin does not add them along it. Insulation is the mechanism of the speed increase, not a drag on it. Myelin surrounds the axon rather than expanding the cytoplasmic core, so the diameter effect is separate.

cards.q: What is saltatory conduction?
cards.a: Action potentials regenerating only at the nodes while current jumps the internodes.
options: Action potentials skipping over the nodes and regenerating under the myelin
Action potentials traveling in both directions away from the trigger zone at once
Action potentials regenerating only at the nodes while current jumps the internodes
Action potentials passing from one axon to a neighboring axon in the nerve
cards.explanation: In a myelinated axon the voltage gated channels sit at the nodes, so the action potential is rebuilt there while the depolarizing current spreads passively and rapidly beneath the insulated internodes, which is what saltatory means. Skipping the nodes reverses the arrangement, since the nodes are the only places with the channels needed to regenerate the signal. Bidirectional spread from a stimulus site is a separate phenomenon and occurs in unmyelinated axons too. Action potentials do not hop between separate axons.

cards.q: In a myelinated axon, where is the action potential regenerated?
cards.a: At the nodes of Ranvier.
options: Beneath the thickest part of the myelin sheath
At the nodes of Ranvier
At the axon terminal only
Uniformly along the entire internode
cards.explanation: Nodes of Ranvier are short gaps in the myelin packed with voltage gated Na+ channels, and they are the only stretches of a myelinated axon where the membrane can produce a fresh action potential. Under the myelin there are almost no voltage gated channels, so nothing can be regenerated there. The axon terminal converts the arriving action potential into transmitter release rather than serving as the site of propagation. Regeneration along the whole internode describes continuous conduction in an unmyelinated axon.

cards.q: Which fiber type conducts action potentials most rapidly?
cards.a: Large diameter myelinated fibers.
options: Small diameter unmyelinated fibers
Large diameter myelinated fibers
Large diameter unmyelinated fibers
Small diameter myelinated fibers
cards.explanation: Speed rises with diameter and with myelination, so the fastest axons in the body combine both, reaching roughly 100 m/s in the largest myelinated fibers that serve proprioception and skeletal muscle. Small unmyelinated fibers sit at the other extreme, near 1 m/s, and carry slow pain and autonomic signals. A small myelinated fiber or a large unmyelinated one has one advantage but not the other, so each falls in between.

cards.q: What does myelin do to current leak across the internodal membrane?
cards.a: It reduces leak, so more current reaches the next node.
options: It has no effect on leak but lowers cytoplasmic resistance
It increases leak, which speeds repolarization at each node
It reduces leak, so more current reaches the next node
It reduces leak only in unmyelinated regions of the axon
cards.explanation: Wrapping the axon in many layers of lipid membrane drastically raises the resistance of the path out of the cell, so the current spreading forward inside the axon stays inside and arrives at the next node with enough strength to reach threshold. Increased leak would be a handicap, draining the very current that has to reach the next node. Myelin acts on the membrane, not on the cytoplasm, so cytoplasmic resistance is unchanged. Describing unmyelinated regions as myelinated is a contradiction.

cards.q: What are typical conduction velocities for the fastest myelinated fibers and for unmyelinated fibers?
cards.a: About 100 m/s and about 1 m/s.
options: About 10 m/s and about 1 m/s
About 100 m/s and about 50 m/s
About 100 m/s and about 1 m/s
About 1000 m/s and about 100 m/s
cards.explanation: Large myelinated fibers reach roughly 100 m/s, while small unmyelinated fibers crawl along near 1 m/s, a hundredfold range that explains why touch reaches awareness long before slow burning pain. A top speed of 10 m/s underestimates the fastest fibers by an order of magnitude. Fifty meters per second is typical of a medium myelinated fiber, not of an unmyelinated one. A thousand meters per second is faster than any biological axon conducts.

cards.q: What is continuous conduction?
cards.a: Sequential regeneration of the action potential at every adjacent patch of membrane.
options: Passive spread of a graded potential along an unmyelinated axon
Sequential regeneration of the action potential at every adjacent patch of membrane
Regeneration of the action potential only at points where Schwann cells are absent
Conduction that continues after the stimulus has been removed
cards.explanation: In an unmyelinated axon, voltage gated channels are spread along the whole membrane, so each small patch depolarizes its neighbor to threshold and the action potential is rebuilt step by step without skipping anything, which is slower than jumping node to node. Passive spread without regeneration describes a graded potential, and it decays rather than propagating. Regeneration at gaps in a sheath describes saltatory conduction in a myelinated axon. Conduction certainly continues past the stimulus, but that is true of any propagating action potential and is not what the term names.

cards.q: Rank these four axons from fastest to slowest: a 20 micrometer myelinated fiber, a 2 micrometer myelinated fiber, a 20 micrometer unmyelinated fiber, and a 1 micrometer unmyelinated fiber.
cards.a: 20 micrometer myelinated, 20 micrometer unmyelinated, 2 micrometer myelinated, 1 micrometer unmyelinated.
options: 1 micrometer unmyelinated, 2 micrometer myelinated, 20 micrometer unmyelinated, 20 micrometer myelinated
20 micrometer myelinated, 20 micrometer unmyelinated, 2 micrometer myelinated, 1 micrometer unmyelinated
2 micrometer myelinated, 20 micrometer myelinated, 1 micrometer unmyelinated, 20 micrometer unmyelinated
20 micrometer unmyelinated, 20 micrometer myelinated, 1 micrometer unmyelinated, 2 micrometer myelinated
cards.explanation: Both factors push in the same direction, so the fiber that is both large and myelinated is fastest and the one that is both small and unmyelinated is slowest, with the two mixed cases in between. The ordering that starts with the 1 micrometer unmyelinated fiber lists the same four in exactly reverse order, slowest first. The two orderings that put a small fiber ahead of a large one with the same insulation contradict the diameter rule. Where the two middle fibers fall relative to each other depends on the exact numbers, but both clearly sit between the extremes.

cards.q: An action potential travels 15 cm along a nerve in 3 ms. What is the conduction velocity?
options: 5 m/s
45 m/s
50 m/s
cards.explanation: Convert first: 15 cm is 0.15 m and 3 ms is 0.003 s, and 0.15 divided by 0.003 gives 50 m/s, a value typical of a medium sized myelinated fiber. Five meters per second would come from dividing 15 by 3 and then mishandling the unit conversion by a factor of ten. Forty five is what you get by subtracting rather than dividing. Five hundred is off by a factor of ten in the other direction and exceeds any biological conduction velocity.

cards.q: A segment of myelin is destroyed along an axon, leaving the underlying membrane intact but with few voltage gated Na+ channels. What happens to conduction there?
cards.a: It slows and may fail, because current leaks out before reaching the next node.
options: It speeds up, because the current no longer has to jump from node to node
It reverses direction when it reaches the damaged segment of the axon
It is unchanged, because the axon still has its normal diameter and gradients
It slows and may fail, because current leaks out before reaching the next node
cards.explanation: The bare stretch has low membrane resistance and almost no voltage gated Na+ channels, so current leaks out across it and the depolarization arriving at the next node may be too small to reach threshold, producing slowing or outright conduction block. Removing myelin removes the insulation that made saltatory conduction fast, so speeding up is the opposite of what occurs. Diameter still matters, but it cannot compensate for the loss of insulation on a channel poor membrane. Nothing about demyelination reverses the direction of travel.

cards.q: Why does saltatory conduction cost less ATP than continuous conduction over the same distance?
cards.a: Fewer ions cross the membrane, so the Na+/K+ ATPase has less to restore.
options: Fewer ions cross the membrane, so the Na+/K+ ATPase has less to restore
Myelin supplies ATP to the axon along the internode
Action potentials in myelinated axons are smaller and use less charge
The axon uses passive diffusion rather than active transport at the nodes
cards.explanation: Ion movement is confined to the small nodal patches rather than occurring over the whole membrane surface, so far less Na+ enters and less K+ leaves per action potential and the pump spends much less ATP restoring the gradients. Myelin is made by supporting cells and insulates the axon; it does not feed it ATP. Action potentials in myelinated axons are full sized, so the savings do not come from smaller signals. The pump uses ATP in both cases, and passive diffusion through channels is what the pump has to reverse.

cards.q: Two axons have the same diameter, but one is myelinated and one is not. Which conducts faster and why?
cards.a: The myelinated one, because insulation lets local current reach the next node quickly.
options: The myelinated one, because insulation lets local current reach the next node quickly
The unmyelinated one, because every patch of its membrane can regenerate the signal
They conduct at the same speed, since diameter is the only factor that matters
The unmyelinated one, because it has less membrane capacitance to charge
cards.explanation: High membrane resistance under the myelin keeps current inside the axon so it spreads rapidly to the next node, and the time consuming step of opening channels happens only at the nodes rather than at every point, so the myelinated axon wins easily. Regenerating at every patch sounds thorough but is exactly what makes continuous conduction slow, since each step takes the same fraction of a millisecond. Diameter matters but is not the only factor. Myelin actually lowers effective membrane capacitance, so the capacitance argument favors the myelinated fiber, not the bare one.

cards.q: A painful stimulus produces a sharp, well localized sensation followed a second later by a dull ache. Which fibers carry each?
cards.a: Fast myelinated A delta fibers first, then slow unmyelinated C fibers.
options: Slow unmyelinated C fibers first, then fast myelinated A delta fibers
Both are carried by A delta fibers, with the delay caused by the refractory period
Both are carried by C fibers, with the delay caused by processing in the brain
Fast myelinated A delta fibers first, then slow unmyelinated C fibers
cards.explanation: A delta fibers are small but myelinated and conduct at roughly 20 m/s, so their signal arrives first as the sharp fast pain, while unmyelinated C fibers conduct near 1 m/s and deliver the dull slow pain a noticeable interval later. Putting the C fibers first ignores that unmyelinated fibers are the slowest in the body. If both sensations came from one fiber type, the delay would have to come from somewhere else, and neither central processing nor the refractory period stretches to a full second.

cards.q: In a myelinated axon, why does the spacing of the nodes of Ranvier matter?
cards.a: Local current must still be above threshold when it reaches the next node.
options: Local current must still be above threshold when it reaches the next node
The Na+/K+ ATPase can only work at evenly spaced intervals
Widely spaced nodes would raise the amplitude of the action potential
Nodes must be spaced closely enough for myelin to remain attached
cards.explanation: Current spreading under the internode decays as it goes, so nodes have to be close enough that the depolarization arriving at the next one is still large enough to open its Na+ channels, and spacing them too far apart causes conduction to fail. The pump is distributed along the membrane and does not require particular spacing. Node spacing does not change action potential amplitude, which is all or none. Myelin attachment is a matter of the supporting cell wrapping the axon, not of a threshold current requirement.

cards.q: A nerve conduction study on a patient shows conduction velocity reduced from 55 m/s to 25 m/s, while the size of the response is nearly normal. What does this pattern suggest?
cards.a: Demyelination, since insulation is lost but the axons themselves are intact.
options: Loss of axons, since fewer fibers would be contributing to the response
A shortened refractory period in the surviving fibers
A rise in threshold at the stimulating electrode
Demyelination, since insulation is lost but the axons themselves are intact
cards.explanation: Velocity depends on insulation and diameter while response size depends on how many axons are firing, so a large drop in speed with a preserved response points to intact axons that have lost myelin. Axon loss would do the reverse, shrinking the response while the surviving fibers still conduct at close to normal speed. A raised stimulating threshold would mean a larger stimulus was needed, not slower conduction once firing occurred. Refractory period sets maximum firing frequency, not the velocity of a single action potential.

cards.q: A signal must travel 1 m from the toe to the spinal cord. Compare the arrival time in an axon conducting at 50 m/s and one conducting at 1 m/s.
cards.a: About 20 ms versus about 1000 ms, a difference of nearly a second.
options: About 20 ms versus about 1000 ms, a difference of nearly a second
About 2 ms versus about 100 ms, a difference of about 98 ms
About 20 ms versus about 100 ms, a difference of 80 ms
About 50 ms versus about 1000 ms, a difference of 950 ms
cards.explanation: Time is distance divided by velocity, so 1 m at 50 m/s takes 0.02 s or 20 ms, and 1 m at 1 m/s takes a full second, which is why slow C fiber pain lags so noticeably behind fast touch from the same spot. The options offering 100 ms for the slow fiber use 10 m/s rather than 1 m/s. Two milliseconds would require 500 m/s. Fifty milliseconds inverts the calculation, multiplying by the velocity instead of dividing.

cards.q: Conduction velocity in a child's motor nerves rises steadily during the first two years of life. What two developmental changes account for this?
cards.a: Progressive myelination and increasing axon diameter.
options: Increasing action potential amplitude and lengthening of the axons
Increasing Na+/K+ ATPase density and rising body temperature
Shortening of the refractory period and rising extracellular K+
Progressive myelination and increasing axon diameter
cards.explanation: Both factors that set conduction velocity are still developing: axons grow thicker, which lowers internal resistance, and supporting cells lay down myelin, which cuts current leak and converts continuous conduction into saltatory conduction. Pump density maintains gradients over time but does not speed a single action potential, and core body temperature is already adult like at birth. Refractory period governs maximum firing rate rather than velocity, and rising extracellular K+ would impair excitability. Action potential amplitude is all or none, and a longer axon adds travel time rather than speed.

cards.q: An axon's diameter doubles. This lowers cytoplasmic resistance but also increases the total membrane surface area available for current leak. Why does conduction still get faster?
cards.a: Internal resistance falls faster than leak rises, so local current reaches farther ahead.
options: Leak does not actually increase, because the membrane thickens as the axon widens
The extra membrane adds voltage gated Na+ channels that speed regeneration
Internal resistance falls faster than leak rises, so local current reaches farther ahead
The larger axon has a lower threshold, so less depolarization is needed downstream
cards.explanation: Internal resistance depends on the cross sectional area, which scales with the square of the radius, while leak depends on the circumference, which scales with the radius alone, so widening the axon helps the internal path more than it hurts the membrane path and the net effect is a longer reach for local current and faster conduction. Membrane thickness is fixed at about the same value in all cells, so it does not compensate. Channel density per unit area stays roughly the same, so extra channels are not the explanation. Threshold is a property of the channels and does not fall with diameter.

cards.q: What is the normal range for plasma K+ concentration?
cards.a: About 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L.
options: About 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L
About 8 to 12 mEq/L
About 135 to 145 mEq/L
About 95 to 105 mEq/L
cards.explanation: Plasma K+ is held in a narrow band near 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L, and even small departures shift the resting potential enough to change excitability in nerve and cardiac muscle. The range of 135 to 145 mEq/L belongs to plasma Na+, and 95 to 105 mEq/L belongs to Cl-. Eight to twelve is close to the intracellular Cl- value and is not a plasma potassium range.

cards.q: Which ion's gradient has the largest influence on the resting membrane potential?
options: Na+
Ca2+
Cl-
K+
cards.explanation: At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K+ than to anything else, so the resting potential sits close to the K+ equilibrium potential and follows changes in extracellular K+ closely. Na+ has a steep gradient but very low resting permeability, so it pulls the resting potential only a little positive of the K+ value. Ca2+ has the steepest gradient of all but almost no resting conductance in a typical axon. Cl- distributes near equilibrium in many cells and tends to follow the potential rather than set it.

cards.q: What is hyperkalemia?
cards.a: An elevated concentration of K+ in the extracellular fluid.
options: An elevated concentration of K+ in the extracellular fluid
An elevated concentration of K+ inside the cell
A reduced concentration of K+ in the extracellular fluid
A reduced concentration of Ca2+ in the extracellular fluid
cards.explanation: Clinical ion names refer to the plasma and extracellular concentration, so hyperkalemia means extracellular K+ is above about 5.0 mEq/L. Intracellular K+ is already high in every cell and is not what the term describes. A reduced extracellular value is hypokalemia, the mirror condition. Reduced extracellular Ca2+ is hypocalcemia, a different ion with a different mechanism of action on excitability.

cards.q: What does hypokalemia do to the resting membrane potential?
cards.a: It makes the resting potential more negative.
options: It makes the resting potential less negative
It makes the resting potential more negative
It leaves the resting potential unchanged
It drives the resting potential above threshold
cards.explanation: Lowering extracellular K+ steepens the K+ gradient, which makes the K+ equilibrium potential more negative, and because the resting membrane follows K+ closely the resting potential is pulled with it, moving the cell farther from threshold. A less negative resting potential is what hyperkalemia produces. The resting potential does change, and quite noticeably, because K+ dominates resting permeability. Nothing about low extracellular K+ drives a cell toward threshold.

cards.q: What does hyperkalemia do to the resting membrane potential?
cards.a: It makes the resting potential less negative.
options: It makes the resting potential more negative
It leaves the resting potential unchanged
It reverses the polarity of the resting potential
It makes the resting potential less negative
cards.explanation: Raising extracellular K+ flattens the K+ gradient, so the K+ equilibrium potential becomes less negative and the resting potential follows it upward toward threshold. A more negative resting potential results from hypokalemia. The resting potential is highly sensitive to extracellular K+, so no change is not an option. Full reversal of polarity requires a large inward current, which nothing in hyperkalemia provides.

cards.q: Local anesthetics such as lidocaine act by blocking which channel?
cards.a: Voltage gated Na+ channels.
options: Voltage gated K+ channels
K+ leak channels
Voltage gated Na+ channels
Chemically gated Cl- channels
cards.explanation: Lidocaine and related drugs bind inside the pore of the voltage gated Na+ channel, so the inward current that drives the upstroke cannot develop and no action potential is generated in the treated nerve. Blocking voltage gated K+ channels would prolong action potentials rather than abolish them. Leak channels set the resting potential and are not the target. Chemically gated Cl- channels are the target of a different class of drugs, and opening rather than blocking them is what produces inhibition.

cards.q: What is the approximate equilibrium potential for K+ in a typical neuron?
cards.a: About -90 mV.
options: About -90 mV
About -70 mV
About -55 mV
About +60 mV
cards.explanation: With roughly 140 mEq/L inside and 4 mEq/L outside, the Nernst equation puts the K+ equilibrium potential near -90 mV, which is the value the membrane approaches during afterhyperpolarization. About -70 mV is the resting potential, which sits positive of the K+ equilibrium potential because of a small Na+ leak. About -55 mV is threshold. About +60 mV is the Na+ equilibrium potential, the target during the upstroke.

cards.q: Which phase of the action potential is abolished first when voltage gated Na+ channels are blocked?
cards.a: The depolarizing upstroke.
options: The afterhyperpolarization
The depolarizing upstroke
The repolarization phase
The resting phase before the stimulus
cards.explanation: The upstroke is carried entirely by Na+ entering through voltage gated Na+ channels, so blocking them removes it, and with no upstroke there is nothing left for the later phases to follow. Afterhyperpolarization and repolarization both depend on K+ channels that open only after a depolarization has occurred, so they disappear as a consequence rather than as the primary effect. The resting phase is maintained by leak channels and the pump and persists whether or not Na+ channels are blocked.

cards.q: Extracellular K+ rises from 4 to 6 mEq/L. Which way does the resting membrane potential move, and what is the immediate effect on excitability?
cards.a: Toward threshold, making the cell more excitable at first.
options: Away from threshold, making the cell less excitable
Toward threshold, making the cell more excitable at first
It does not move, so excitability is unchanged
Toward threshold, but the cell becomes less excitable immediately
cards.explanation: A smaller K+ gradient means a less negative K+ equilibrium potential, so the resting potential drifts up from about -70 mV toward threshold and a smaller stimulus now suffices, which is why mild hyperkalemia is initially excitatory. Moving away from threshold is what hypokalemia does. The resting potential is very sensitive to extracellular K+, so no change is wrong. Reduced excitability does come later, but only once the depolarization is large enough to inactivate Na+ channels.

cards.q: Extracellular K+ reaches 7.5 mEq/L and the resting potential settles near -55 mV. Why does the cell become inexcitable rather than fire continuously?
cards.a: Sustained depolarization inactivates the voltage gated Na+ channels.
options: The K+ equilibrium potential is now above threshold
The Na+/K+ ATPase stops working when extracellular K+ is this high
Sustained depolarization inactivates the voltage gated Na+ channels
Threshold rises above the new resting potential
cards.explanation: Inactivation gates close in response to depolarization and reopen only on repolarization, so a membrane held near threshold accumulates inactivated Na+ channels until too few are available to generate an upstroke, and the cell falls silent despite sitting close to threshold. The K+ equilibrium potential has moved up but is still well below threshold. The pump actually works faster with more extracellular K+, since K+ is its substrate on the outside. Threshold itself does not move; what changes is how many Na+ channels can respond when it is reached.

cards.q: A patient's plasma K+ falls to 2.5 mEq/L. Predict the effect on nerve and muscle excitability.
cards.a: Reduced excitability, because the resting potential moves farther from threshold.
options: Increased excitability, because the K+ gradient across the membrane is steeper
Reduced excitability, because the Na+ channels have become inactivated
No change, because intracellular K+ is unchanged by the plasma value
Reduced excitability, because the resting potential moves farther from threshold
cards.explanation: Lower extracellular K+ makes the K+ equilibrium potential more negative and hyperpolarizes the cell, so a larger depolarization is needed to reach threshold and the cell is harder to excite. A steeper K+ gradient does hyperpolarize the cell, but hyperpolarization reduces excitability rather than increasing it. Intracellular K+ is indeed nearly unchanged, but the resting potential depends on the ratio across the membrane, so the outside value matters enormously. Na+ channel inactivation is the mechanism in hyperkalemia, not hypokalemia; here the channels are, if anything, more available than usual.

cards.q: Lidocaine is injected around a sensory nerve. What happens to the receptor potential at the sensory ending and to the action potentials in the axon?
cards.a: The receptor potential still forms, but no action potentials are generated.
options: Both the receptor potential and the resulting action potentials are abolished
Both continue, but the action potentials are smaller than normal
The receptor potential is abolished but action potentials continue
The receptor potential still forms, but no action potentials are generated
cards.explanation: Receptor potentials come from mechanically or chemically gated channels, which lidocaine does not block, so the local graded response survives, but without voltage gated Na+ channels that depolarization can never be converted into a propagating action potential and nothing reaches the central nervous system. Abolishing both would require blocking the sensory transduction channels as well. Losing the receptor potential while keeping action potentials reverses the order of events in the pathway. Smaller action potentials would occur with partial block, but a full block produces none at all.

cards.q: A cell is bathed in a solution with extracellular K+ lowered from 4 to 2 mEq/L. Which way does the K+ equilibrium potential move?
cards.a: It becomes more negative.
options: It becomes more negative
It becomes less negative
It becomes positive
It does not change, since intracellular K+ is unchanged
cards.explanation: The Nernst equation depends on the ratio of outside to inside concentration, and halving the outside value makes that ratio smaller, driving the equilibrium potential further below zero, toward roughly -108 mV. Becoming less negative is the direction taken when extracellular K+ rises. A positive value would require extracellular K+ to exceed intracellular K+, which is far from the case. Holding intracellular K+ constant does not protect the equilibrium potential, because the ratio is what matters.

cards.q: Which single measurement best distinguishes a cell in hyperkalemia from a cell in hypokalemia?
cards.a: The resting membrane potential.
options: The peak of the action potential
The resting membrane potential
The conduction velocity of the axon
The duration of the absolute refractory period
cards.explanation: The two conditions push the resting potential in opposite directions, depolarized in hyperkalemia and hyperpolarized in hypokalemia, so the baseline voltage separates them immediately. The action potential peak can fall in hyperkalemia through Na+ channel inactivation, but it does not move in a clean opposite direction in hypokalemia. Conduction velocity and refractory duration can both be affected indirectly, but neither gives the clear, opposite signed answer that the resting potential does.

cards.q: A patient's plasma K+ climbs steadily from 5 to 7 mEq/L. Describe how excitability changes over that climb.
cards.a: It rises at first as the resting potential nears threshold, then falls as Na+ channels inactivate.
options: It falls steadily throughout, because K+ always stabilizes the membrane
It rises steadily throughout, because the resting potential just keeps approaching threshold
It rises at first as the resting potential nears threshold, then falls as Na+ channels inactivate
It is unchanged until K+ exceeds 10 mEq/L, when the cell suddenly depolarizes
cards.explanation: Two effects overlap: bringing the resting potential closer to threshold makes firing easier, but holding the membrane depolarized progressively inactivates Na+ channels, and beyond a point the second effect dominates and the cell cannot fire at all. Steady loss of excitability throughout ignores the early phase, which is why rising K+ can first cause tingling and cramping. Steady gain throughout is the classic half learned answer, since it tracks only the distance to threshold and forgets inactivation. Excitability changes measurably well before 10 mEq/L, so a sudden all or nothing switch does not describe the progression.

cards.q: A dentist injects lidocaine near a sensory nerve before drilling. Trace what happens from the stimulus to the perceived sensation.
cards.a: Receptor potentials still form, but the axon cannot generate action potentials.
options: The receptors no longer respond, so no receptor potential and no signal are produced
Action potentials still travel but arrive too slowly to be perceived as pain
Receptor potentials still form, but the axon cannot generate action potentials
The brain receives the signal but cannot interpret it because the fibers are blocked
cards.explanation: Drilling still deforms and damages tissue, so transduction channels still open and a graded receptor potential still develops, but with voltage gated Na+ channels blocked the trigger zone cannot convert that depolarization into a propagating action potential, and the pathway falls silent at that step. The receptors themselves use chemically and mechanically gated channels that lidocaine does not affect. Slower conduction would delay the sensation rather than abolish it. Nothing reaches the brain at all, so an interpretation problem in the brain is not the issue.

cards.q: An axon in an experimental bath has a resting potential of -60 mV instead of -70 mV, and its action potentials have a lower peak than normal. Which change to the bath explains both findings?
cards.a: Extracellular K+ has been raised.
options: Extracellular Na+ has been raised
Extracellular K+ has been raised
Extracellular Cl- has been lowered
Extracellular K+ has been lowered
cards.explanation: Raising extracellular K+ makes the K+ equilibrium potential less negative and depolarizes the resting membrane, and that sustained depolarization inactivates a fraction of the Na+ channels so fewer are available for the upstroke, which lowers the peak, so one change accounts for both observations. Raising extracellular Na+ would raise the peak rather than lower it and would barely touch the resting potential. Lowering Cl- has little effect in an axon where Cl- carries small resting current. Lowering K+ would hyperpolarize the cell, moving the resting potential the wrong way.

cards.q: Extracellular Na+ is halved in a nerve bath. Predict the effect on the resting potential and on the action potential peak.
cards.a: The resting potential barely moves, but the peak falls noticeably.
options: The resting potential barely moves, but the peak falls noticeably
The resting potential falls sharply while the peak is unchanged
Both the resting potential and the peak fall sharply
Neither value changes, because the pump restores the gradient
cards.explanation: Membrane potential at any moment reflects the equilibrium potential of the most permeant ion, so at rest, when K+ permeability rules, cutting extracellular Na+ has only a small effect, while at the peak, when Na+ permeability rules, the less positive Na+ equilibrium potential pulls the peak down noticeably. Equal effects on both would require Na+ to dominate permeability at rest, which it does not. A large fall in resting potential with an unchanged peak reverses which phase depends on Na+. The pump moves ions across the membrane and cannot change what is dissolved in the bath.

cards.q: In a neuron simulation, tetrodotoxin (TTX) is applied. Which channel does it block?
cards.a: Voltage gated Na+ channels.
options: K+ leak channels
Voltage gated K+ channels
Voltage gated Na+ channels
The Na+/K+ ATPase
cards.explanation: TTX plugs the pore of the voltage gated Na+ channel, which is why it is the standard tool for removing the depolarizing upstroke in a simulation. Voltage gated K+ channels are blocked by tetraethylammonium instead. Leak channels are not the target of either classic blocker. The Na+/K+ ATPase is inhibited by ouabain, a different agent working on a pump rather than a channel.

cards.q: In a neuron simulation, tetraethylammonium (TEA) is applied. Which channel does it block?
cards.a: Voltage gated K+ channels.
options: Voltage gated Na+ channels
Chemically gated Na+ channels
Voltage gated K+ channels
Voltage gated Ca2+ channels
cards.explanation: TEA blocks the delayed rectifier voltage gated K+ channel, so in a simulation it is used to slow repolarization and remove the afterhyperpolarization. Voltage gated Na+ channels are the target of tetrodotoxin. Chemically gated channels respond to transmitter and are not part of the axonal action potential machinery being tested. Voltage gated Ca2+ channels matter at the axon terminal but do not shape the axonal action potential in these simulations.

cards.q: In an action potential simulation, what does the stimulus setting control?
cards.a: The size of the depolarization delivered to the membrane.
options: The number of Na+ channels present in the membrane
The size of the depolarization delivered to the membrane
The resting potential the membrane returns to
The conduction velocity of the simulated axon
cards.explanation: The stimulus control sets how large a depolarizing current is injected, which determines whether the membrane reaches threshold and, with repeated stimuli, how often it fires. Channel numbers are properties of the simulated membrane, adjusted separately or by applying a blocker. The resting potential is set by the ion concentrations and leak permeabilities in the model. Conduction velocity depends on the modeled diameter and myelination, not on how hard the membrane is pushed.

cards.q: On a simulated action potential tracing, what does the vertical axis show?
cards.a: Membrane potential in millivolts.
options: Stimulus current in milliamperes
Membrane potential in millivolts
Ion concentration in mEq/L
Channel conductance in siemens
cards.explanation: The standard action potential tracing plots membrane potential in millivolts against time in milliseconds, so the vertical excursion from about -70 mV up to about +30 mV is the action potential itself. Stimulus current is what the experimenter sets, and it appears as an input rather than as the plotted response. Ion concentrations change negligibly during an action potential and are not what the trace displays. Conductance curves can be plotted separately in some simulations but are not the default trace.

cards.q: On a normal simulated tracing, what value does the peak of the action potential reach?
cards.a: About +30 mV.
options: About -55 mV
About -30 mV
About +90 mV
About +30 mV
cards.explanation: A healthy simulated neuron peaks near +30 mV, short of the Na+ equilibrium potential because K+ channels open and Na+ channels inactivate before the membrane gets there. About -55 mV is the threshold line on the same plot, not the peak. About -30 mV is a point on the rising phase. About +90 mV exceeds the Na+ equilibrium potential and is not reachable.

cards.q: In a simulation, a suprathreshold stimulus is delivered and the trace shows only a small bump that decays back to the resting potential. What does this indicate?
cards.a: No action potential was generated.
options: An action potential of reduced amplitude was generated
The resting potential has shifted to a new value
An action potential was generated but conducted away before recording
No action potential was generated
cards.explanation: A small decaying bump is the passive response of the membrane to injected current, a graded potential, and the absence of any regenerative upstroke means no action potential occurred. A reduced amplitude action potential would still show a clear rapid rise and fall rather than a passive decay. A recording electrode on the stimulated membrane sees the action potential where it starts, so conduction away is not an explanation. The trace returns to its original baseline, so the resting potential has not shifted.

cards.q: In an action potential simulation, what does the threshold stimulus mean?
cards.a: The smallest stimulus that produces an action potential.
options: The stimulus that produces the largest action potential
The smallest stimulus that produces an action potential
The stimulus that produces the fastest conduction velocity
The stimulus that produces the shortest refractory period
cards.explanation: Threshold stimulus is found by increasing the stimulus in small steps until an action potential first appears, and that value marks the boundary between subthreshold and suprathreshold. Since action potentials are all or none, no stimulus produces a larger one, so a stimulus that yields the largest action potential is something that does not exist. Conduction velocity and refractory period are properties of the membrane and are not set by the size of the stimulus.

cards.q: Which phase of the simulated action potential does TEA prolong?
cards.a: Repolarization.
options: Repolarization
The rising phase to the peak
The resting phase before the stimulus
The delay between the stimulus and threshold
cards.explanation: Repolarization is driven by K+ leaving through voltage gated K+ channels, so blocking those channels with TEA removes the main outward current and the membrane takes much longer to return toward rest. The rising phase depends on Na+ entry and is unaffected by a K+ channel blocker. The resting phase is maintained by leak channels rather than by the voltage gated K+ channels TEA blocks. The delay to threshold depends on the stimulus size and on passive membrane properties.

cards.q: TTX is added in the simulation and a stimulus well above the previous threshold is delivered. What does the tracing show?
cards.a: A small passive depolarization with no action potential.
options: A normal action potential with a delayed onset
A small passive depolarization with no action potential
An action potential with a normal peak but slow repolarization
An action potential with a reduced peak and a normal afterhyperpolarization
cards.explanation: With voltage gated Na+ channels blocked there is no regenerative inward current, so the injected stimulus produces only the passive depolarization it delivers directly and the membrane decays back to rest. A delayed but normal action potential would require working Na+ channels. Slow repolarization with a normal peak is the TEA pattern, since it leaves the Na+ channels intact. A reduced peak is what partial Na+ block produces, but a full block leaves no action potential at all.

cards.q: TEA is added in the simulation and a suprathreshold stimulus is delivered. What does the tracing show?
cards.a: A normal upstroke with slowed repolarization and little afterhyperpolarization.
options: A normal upstroke with slowed repolarization and little afterhyperpolarization
No response beyond the stimulus artifact, with the membrane staying at rest
A reduced upstroke with normal repolarization and normal afterhyperpolarization
A normal upstroke followed by a deeper and longer afterhyperpolarization
cards.explanation: TEA leaves the Na+ channels untouched, so the upstroke is normal, but removing the delayed K+ current slows the return to rest and eliminates the overshoot below rest that those same lingering K+ channels normally cause. No response at all is the TTX pattern. A reduced upstroke would point to a Na+ channel problem instead. A deeper afterhyperpolarization would require more K+ efflux, which is the opposite of what a K+ channel blocker does.

cards.q: With TTX present, the simulated stimulus is increased fivefold and still produces no action potential. How should this be interpreted?
cards.a: The block is on the channels themselves, so no stimulus size can restore firing.
options: The stimulus is still below the new threshold and should be raised further
The membrane is in a refractory period that a stronger stimulus will overcome
The recording electrode has failed and should be repositioned
The block is on the channels themselves, so no stimulus size can restore firing
cards.explanation: Threshold has meaning only if Na+ channels are available to carry the regenerative current, and when those channels are plugged the membrane can be depolarized as far as you like without an action potential ever developing. Raising the stimulus further is the intuitive move but it cannot work, and recognizing that is the point of the experiment. The electrode is clearly working, since the passive depolarization is recorded. The membrane is not refractory, because no action potential preceded this stimulus.

cards.q: A simulated tracing shows a normal resting potential and a normal time course, but the peak reaches only +5 mV instead of +30 mV. What is the most likely cause?
cards.a: A fraction of the voltage gated Na+ channels is blocked.
options: A fraction of the voltage gated K+ channels is blocked
The stimulus was delivered below threshold
The Na+/K+ ATPase has been inhibited
A fraction of the voltage gated Na+ channels is blocked
cards.explanation: The height of the peak depends on how much Na+ current the membrane can generate, so removing some of the Na+ channels lowers the peak while leaving the overall shape and timing recognizable. Blocking K+ channels would stretch repolarization rather than shorten the climb. Inhibiting the pump degrades gradients over minutes and would show up first as a drifting resting potential. A subthreshold stimulus would give no action potential at all rather than a small one, since the response is all or none.

cards.q: A simulated action potential has a normal peak and normal repolarization but no afterhyperpolarization at all. Which manipulation best explains this?
cards.a: Partial block of the voltage gated K+ channels.
options: Partial block of the voltage gated Na+ channels
An increase in extracellular Na+
Partial block of the voltage gated K+ channels
A decrease in extracellular Na+
cards.explanation: Afterhyperpolarization exists because voltage gated K+ channels remain open past the return to rest, so reducing their number removes the extra K+ efflux and the trace stops at the resting potential, and a partial block can do this while leaving repolarization close to normal. Na+ channel block would show up in the upstroke and the peak. Changing extracellular Na+ shifts the peak by changing the Na+ equilibrium potential and does not selectively remove the tail of the trace.

cards.q: In the simulation, the stimulus is increased from just above threshold to three times threshold, and repeated stimuli are delivered. What changes on the tracing?
cards.a: The action potentials come closer together while keeping the same height.
options: The action potentials become taller while keeping the same spacing
The action potentials come closer together while keeping the same height
The action potentials become wider while keeping the same height
The action potentials arrive at the recording site sooner after leaving the trigger zone
cards.explanation: Stronger stimulation drives the membrane back to threshold sooner after each recovery, so the frequency rises while each action potential stays the same size, which is the simulation demonstrating frequency coding. Taller action potentials would violate the all or none principle. Width is set by channel kinetics and does not change with stimulus strength. Conduction time depends on the axon's cable properties, not on how hard the trigger zone is pushed.

cards.q: A simulated response grows steadily as the stimulus is increased and never rises above 0 mV. What is being recorded?
cards.a: A graded potential rather than an action potential.
options: A graded potential rather than an action potential
An action potential with partial Na+ channel block
An action potential recorded far from the trigger zone
An afterhyperpolarization following a subthreshold stimulus
cards.explanation: Growing in proportion to the stimulus is the definition of a graded response, and the absence of any overshoot confirms that the regenerative Na+ current never took over. A partially blocked action potential has a lower peak but is still all or none, so it does not scale smoothly with the stimulus. Action potentials are the same size wherever along the axon they are recorded, so distance does not explain a graded response. Afterhyperpolarization is a hyperpolarization and requires a preceding action potential.

cards.q: A simulation applies enough TTX to block half the Na+ channels. Predict what happens to the threshold stimulus and to the peak of the action potentials that still occur.
cards.a: Threshold rises and the peak falls, because less Na+ current is available.
options: Threshold falls and the peak rises, because the remaining channels open more readily
Threshold is unchanged and the peak falls, since threshold depends only on voltage
Threshold rises and the peak falls, because less Na+ current is available
Threshold rises and the peak is unchanged, since amplitude is all or none
cards.explanation: With half the channels gone, more depolarization is needed before the inward current can outrun the outward one, so the stimulus required rises, and the total inward current available at any voltage is smaller, so the peak is lower. The remaining channels have unchanged gating and do not compensate by opening more readily. Threshold is a voltage, but which voltage is enough depends on the density of available channels, so it does shift. All or none applies to a given membrane in a given state, and a state with fewer Na+ channels has a lower all or none amplitude.

cards.q: TEA is applied and the simulated neuron is then driven with rapid repeated stimuli. Predict the effect on the maximum firing frequency.
cards.a: It falls, because the prolonged action potential lengthens the refractory period.
options: It rises, because K+ channels no longer oppose depolarization
It is unchanged, because firing frequency is set by the stimulus strength alone
It falls, because the prolonged action potential lengthens the refractory period
It falls, because the action potential amplitude is reduced
cards.explanation: Na+ channels can only recover from inactivation once the membrane repolarizes, so a trace that takes far longer to come back down keeps the membrane refractory for longer and the next action potential cannot start as soon, lowering the ceiling on firing rate. The removal of an opposing outward current does make it easier to depolarize, but the rate limiting step is recovery from inactivation, not the ease of depolarizing. Stimulus strength drives the rate toward the ceiling but does not set the ceiling. Amplitude is essentially preserved with TEA, since the Na+ channels are untouched.

cards.q: A simulated tracing shows a normal upstroke and peak, repolarization taking three times as long as the control, and no afterhyperpolarization. Which blocker was used?
cards.a: A voltage gated K+ channel blocker such as TEA.
options: A voltage gated K+ channel blocker such as TEA
A voltage gated Na+ channel blocker such as TTX
A Na+/K+ ATPase inhibitor such as ouabain
A blocker of chemically gated channels at the synapse
cards.explanation: Reading the trace backward, an intact upstroke and peak clear the Na+ channels of suspicion, while slowed repolarization and a missing afterhyperpolarization both point at the delayed K+ current that normally ends the action potential. TTX would have removed the action potential entirely rather than stretching its tail. Pump inhibition acts over minutes and would show as a drifting baseline rather than a reshaped single action potential. Chemically gated channels are at synapses and play no part in shaping the axonal waveform.

cards.q: Both TTX and TEA are applied to the simulated neuron at once, then a large stimulus is delivered. What does the tracing show and why?
cards.a: A passive depolarization only, since without Na+ channels nothing can start.
options: A passive depolarization only, since without Na+ channels nothing can start
A prolonged action potential, because the K+ channel block dominates the result
A normal action potential, because the two blockers cancel each other out
A hyperpolarization, because K+ efflux is left unopposed by Na+ entry
cards.explanation: The Na+ current is the event that starts everything, so removing it means there is nothing for the K+ block to prolong and the trace shows only the passive response to the injected current. A prolonged action potential requires an action potential to exist in the first place. The two blockers act on different channels and cannot cancel; each removes a current, and neither restores the other. A K+ block reduces efflux rather than leaving it unopposed, so a hyperpolarization is the wrong direction.

cards.q: What is a compound action potential?
cards.a: The summed electrical response of all the axons in a nerve.
options: The graded potential recorded at a sensory ending
A single action potential recorded from one large axon
An action potential that travels in both directions at once
The summed electrical response of all the axons in a nerve
cards.explanation: A nerve contains many axons, and a surface electrode records the sum of their individual action potentials as one wave, which is why it is called compound. A recording from one axon is a single unit action potential and is all or none. Bidirectional travel can occur after mid nerve stimulation but is not what the term describes. A graded potential at a sensory ending is a receptor potential, recorded at a single ending rather than from a whole nerve.

cards.q: Is the compound action potential all or none?
cards.a: No, its size grows as more axons are recruited by a stronger stimulus.
options: Yes, because each axon in the nerve is all or none
No, because each axon fires with a different amplitude
Yes, because the whole nerve either fires together or does not fire
No, its size grows as more axons are recruited by a stronger stimulus
cards.explanation: Every individual axon is all or none, but axons have different thresholds, so a stronger stimulus brings more of them into the response and the summed wave grows, which makes the compound response graded. Reasoning from the behavior of one axon to the behavior of the whole nerve is the trap here. The nerve does not fire as a unit; each axon decides independently. Individual axons do not vary in amplitude; the variation in the compound response comes from how many are firing.

cards.q: How is conduction velocity calculated from a nerve recording?
cards.a: Distance traveled divided by conduction time.
options: Distance traveled divided by conduction time
Conduction time divided by distance traveled
Distance traveled multiplied by conduction time
Stimulus strength divided by conduction time
cards.explanation: Velocity is distance per unit time, so measuring how far the signal traveled and how long it took gives the answer directly, usually reported in meters per second. Dividing time by distance gives the reciprocal, which is a delay per unit length rather than a velocity. Multiplying the two gives a quantity with no physical meaning here. Stimulus strength determines how many axons fire, not how fast the action potentials travel.

cards.q: What is latency in a nerve conduction recording?
cards.a: The time from the stimulus to the onset of the recorded response.
options: The time from the peak of the recorded response back to baseline
The time from the stimulus to the onset of the recorded response
The duration of the compound action potential itself
The interval between two successive stimuli
cards.explanation: Latency is the delay between delivering the stimulus and seeing the response arrive at the recording electrode, and it is the raw measurement from which conduction velocity is calculated. The fall from peak to baseline is part of the waveform's shape rather than its arrival time. The duration of the wave reflects the spread of fiber velocities in the nerve. The interval between stimuli is set by the experimenter and is a separate parameter.

cards.q: Which axons contribute to the earliest part of a compound action potential?
cards.a: The largest myelinated axons.
options: The smallest unmyelinated axons
The axons closest to the recording electrode
The largest myelinated axons
The axons with the lowest resting potential
cards.explanation: The earliest arrival belongs to the fastest fibers, and the fastest fibers are the large myelinated ones, so the leading edge of the compound response reflects them. Small unmyelinated axons are the slowest and contribute to the late, low components of the wave. All the axons in a nerve travel essentially the same distance to the electrode, so proximity does not sort the arrivals. Resting potential differences affect excitability rather than conduction speed.

cards.q: In what units is nerve conduction velocity usually reported?
cards.a: Meters per second.
options: Meters per second
Millivolts per millisecond
Milliseconds per centimeter
Millimeters per minute
cards.explanation: Conduction velocity is a speed and is conventionally given in meters per second, which puts human nerves in a convenient range of roughly 1 to 100 m/s. Millivolts per millisecond is a rate of voltage change, which describes the steepness of the upstroke rather than travel speed. Milliseconds per centimeter is a delay per unit length, the reciprocal of velocity. Millimeters per minute is a speed but on a timescale suited to growth rather than to electrical signaling.

cards.q: Why does a compound action potential often show more than one peak?
cards.a: Because groups of fibers with different conduction velocities arrive at different times.
options: Because each axon fires more than once per stimulus
Because groups of fibers with different conduction velocities arrive at different times
Because the stimulus is delivered more than once
Because the recording electrode picks up both the depolarization and the repolarization
cards.explanation: A nerve carries fiber groups with very different diameters and degrees of myelination, and each group arrives as its own bump, so the summed wave separates into peaks as the recording distance grows. A single stimulus produces one action potential per axon, so repeated firing is not the explanation. Multiple stimuli would be visible as multiple stimulus artifacts. Depolarization and repolarization within one wave shape a single deflection rather than producing separate peaks.

cards.q: What is the stimulus artifact on a nerve conduction tracing?
cards.a: The stimulator current picked up directly by the recording electrode.
options: The first action potentials arriving from the fastest fibers in the nerve
Noise from the muscle beneath the electrode contracting after the stimulus
The stimulator current picked up directly by the recording electrode
The afterhyperpolarization that follows the compound action potential
cards.explanation: Current from the stimulator spreads through the tissue and reaches the recording electrode almost instantly, producing a sharp deflection that marks time zero for measuring latency. The arrival of the fastest fibers comes after a real conduction delay and is the response, not the artifact. Muscle activity produces its own later potentials and is a different signal. Afterhyperpolarization follows the response rather than preceding it.

cards.q: Two recording sites are 12 cm apart and the response onset differs by 2 ms between them. What is the conduction velocity of the fastest fibers?
options: 6 m/s
24 m/s
60 m/s
cards.explanation: Convert to base units first: 12 cm is 0.12 m and 2 ms is 0.002 s, and 0.12 divided by 0.002 is 60 m/s, a normal value for a large myelinated nerve. Six meters per second comes from dropping a factor of ten in the length conversion. Twenty four comes from multiplying rather than dividing. Six hundred exceeds any biological conduction velocity by roughly a factor of six.

cards.q: Why is conduction velocity usually calculated from the difference between two recording sites rather than from a single latency?
cards.a: Subtracting removes the fixed delay before conduction actually begins.
options: Subtracting cancels out the effect of temperature on the nerve fibers
Subtracting removes the fixed delay before conduction actually begins
A single site cannot detect the compound action potential reliably enough
Two sites are needed because each one records only half of the fibers
cards.explanation: Some of the latency at any single site is spent getting the axons to fire in the first place, and that delay is the same at both sites, so subtracting the two latencies leaves only the time spent traveling the known distance between them. Temperature does affect conduction, but it affects both sites equally and is not what the subtraction is designed to remove. One electrode records the compound response perfectly well; the problem is interpreting its latency. Both electrodes see the same population of fibers, just at different times.

cards.q: The stimulus to a nerve is increased and the compound action potential grows larger. What does this show?
cards.a: More axons are being recruited into the response.
options: Each axon is producing a larger action potential
The axons are conducting more rapidly
More axons are being recruited into the response
The refractory period has shortened
cards.explanation: Individual axons are all or none, so the only way the summed wave can grow is for additional axons, with higher thresholds, to start contributing. Larger individual action potentials are ruled out by the all or none principle. Conduction velocity is a fixed property of each axon and does not rise with stimulus strength. Refractory period is a membrane property and is not affected by how hard the nerve is stimulated.

cards.q: A compound action potential is recorded first at 4 cm and then at 20 cm from the stimulus site. How does the shape of the wave change with distance?
cards.a: It spreads out and flattens as the fiber groups separate in time.
options: It becomes taller and narrower as the signal builds
It stays exactly the same, since action potentials do not decay
It spreads out and flattens as the fiber groups separate in time
It reverses polarity because the electrode is now past the fastest fibers
cards.explanation: Fast and slow fibers start together but pull apart as they travel, so at longer distances their contributions no longer overlap and the summed wave becomes broader and lower, a phenomenon called temporal dispersion. The wave does not build with distance; each axon carries the same action potential the whole way. It is true that individual action potentials do not decay, but the compound wave still changes shape because of differences in arrival time. Polarity depends on electrode arrangement, not on distance.

cards.q: A nerve conducts at 50 m/s. How long does a signal take to travel 0.5 m?
cards.a: 10 ms.
options: 1 ms
10 ms
25 ms
100 ms
cards.explanation: Time is distance divided by velocity, so 0.5 m divided by 50 m/s gives 0.01 s, which is 10 ms. One millisecond would require a velocity of 500 m/s. Twenty five milliseconds comes from multiplying 0.5 by 50 and misplacing the units. One hundred milliseconds corresponds to a velocity of 5 m/s, which is ten times too slow for this nerve.

cards.q: Which point on the compound action potential should be used to calculate the velocity of the fastest fibers?
cards.a: The onset of the response.
options: The onset of the response
The peak of the response
The point where the response returns to baseline
The midpoint of the falling phase
cards.explanation: The fastest fibers are the first to arrive, so the very beginning of the deflection marks their arrival time and is the correct point for calculating their velocity. The peak reflects the arrival of the largest group of fibers rather than the quickest ones. The return to baseline marks the arrival of the slowest contributors. The falling phase midpoint has no clear physiological meaning as an arrival time.

cards.q: A compound action potential recorded 12 cm from the stimulus begins at 2 ms and its last component arrives at 6 ms. What are the velocities of the fastest and slowest contributing fibers?
cards.a: About 60 m/s and about 20 m/s.
options: About 6 m/s and about 2 m/s
About 60 m/s and about 20 m/s
About 20 m/s and about 60 m/s
About 24 m/s and about 72 m/s
cards.explanation: Each velocity is 0.12 m divided by the relevant time, so 0.12 divided by 0.002 gives 60 m/s for the earliest arrivals and 0.12 divided by 0.006 gives 20 m/s for the last, a range consistent with a mix of large and medium myelinated fibers. The values near 6 and 2 m/s drop a factor of ten in the length conversion. Assigning 20 m/s to the fastest fibers reverses the relationship, since arriving earlier means moving faster. The pair near 24 and 72 m/s comes from multiplying instead of dividing.

cards.q: One nerve study shows a conduction velocity of 25 m/s with a compound response of near normal size. Another shows a velocity of 52 m/s with a compound response one third of normal size. What does each pattern suggest?
cards.a: The first suggests demyelination and the second suggests loss of axons.
options: The first suggests loss of axons and the second suggests demyelination
Both suggest loss of axons, differing only in severity
Both suggest demyelination, differing only in severity
The first suggests demyelination and the second suggests loss of axons
cards.explanation: Velocity reports the quality of insulation and fiber size, while response amplitude reports how many axons are firing, so slow conduction with a full sized response points to intact axons that have lost myelin, and normal speed with a small response points to fewer surviving axons that still conduct normally. Swapping the two interpretations ignores which measurement each pathology affects. Calling both demyelination cannot explain the reduced amplitude in the second study. Calling both axon loss cannot explain the slowing in the first.

cards.q: A student calculates conduction velocity by dividing the distance from the stimulator to a single recording electrode by the latency at that electrode. How will the result compare with the true velocity?
cards.a: It will be an underestimate, because the latency includes a delay before conduction begins.
options: It will be an underestimate, because the latency includes a delay before conduction begins
It will be an overestimate, because the latency omits the time spent at the nodes
It will be correct, because the delay is negligible in a healthy nerve
It will be an underestimate, because the distance was measured along a curved path in the limb
cards.explanation: Part of the measured latency is spent bringing the axons to threshold rather than traveling, so dividing the full distance by a latency that includes that extra time makes the nerve look slower than it is, which is exactly why two site subtraction is the standard method. The nodal delays are part of conduction and are already included in a true velocity measurement. The initiation delay is a fraction of a millisecond but is a substantial share of a short latency, so it is not negligible. Path curvature is a real measurement concern but would make the assumed distance too short and the velocity too low for a different reason, and it is not the systematic error the single site method introduces.

cards.q: Stimulus intensity is raised step by step, and beyond a certain point the compound action potential stops growing. What has happened, and what is the stimulus called at that point?
cards.a: Every axon in the nerve is now firing, and the stimulus is supramaximal.
options: Every axon in the nerve is now firing, and the stimulus is supramaximal
The axons have reached their maximum action potential amplitude, and the stimulus is at threshold
The nerve has entered a refractory period, and the stimulus is subthreshold
The recording electrode has saturated, and the stimulus is maximal
cards.explanation: The compound response grows only through recruitment, so once the highest threshold axons have been brought in there is nothing left to add and further increases in stimulus change nothing, which is why nerve studies deliberately use a supramaximal stimulus to guarantee a complete response. Individual action potentials never grow with stimulus strength, so a ceiling on amplitude per axon is not the explanation. Threshold names the stimulus that first excites the most sensitive axons, at the other end of the range. Nothing here indicates refractoriness or an equipment limit.
